ROWELL (President of the Council): In order to expedite the introduction into the House of the Pension Bill which the Special Committee on Pensions has already 'reported upon, I would like to ask the unanimous consent of the House to place upon the Order Paper for this day, under Government Orders, the resolutions providing pensions to or in respect of members of the Canadian Naval, Military and Air Forces who served in the war that began in August, 1914, and who were killed or suffered disability while so serving.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This can only be done by unanimous consent.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolutions, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide pensions to or in respect of members of the Canadian Naval, Military and Air Forces, who served in the war that began
in August, 1914, and who were killed or suffered disability while so serving; and therein to provide,-
1.	That there shall be a commission to be known as The Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada, to consist of three commissioners appointed by the Governor in Council.
(a)	Each commissioner shall hold office for ten years, but shall be removable at any time for cause; he shall cease to hold office upon reaching the age of seventy years, and, if not disqualified by age, shall be eligible for reappointment ;
(b)	One of the commissioners shall be appointed iby the Governor in Council to be Chairman of the Commission;
(c)	The commissioners shall devote the whole of their time to their duties under the proposed Act, and shall not accept or hold any office or employment inconsistent therewith.
2.	That the Chairman of the Commission shall be paid a salary of seven thousand dollars per annum, and each of the other commissioners shall be paid a salary of five thousand dollars per annum. Such salaries shall be paid monthly out of any unappropriated moneys forming part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
3.	That the salaries or other remuneration of the officers, clerks and employees of the commission, and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of the proposed Act, shall be paid out of moneys to be provided by Parliament.
4.	That the commission shall award pensions to or in respect of members of the forces who have suffered disability in accordance with Schedule A hereto.
5.	That the commission shall award pensions to or in respect of members of the forces who have died, in accordance with Schedule B hereto.
6.	That the commission shall also have power to pay pensions, allowances and gratuities or other grants awarded in virtue of the Militia Pension Act, or any amendment to that Act, or awarded to or in respect of members of those forces who served in connection with the Fenian Raids or the Northwest Rebellion.
7.	That the Governor in Council may transfer to the commission full power and authority and exclusive jurisdiction to consider, award, pay, administer and deal with any pensions, allowances, gratuities or other grants authorized by any other statute or law of Canada.
8.	That when a person who was domiciled and resident in Canada at the beginning of the war has been awarded a smaller pension than he would have been entitled to under this proposed Act for a disability incurred during the war in any of His Majesty's naval, military or air forces other than the naval, military or air forces of Canada, he shall, on resuming his residence in Canada and during the continuance of such residence, be entitled to such additional pension as will make the total of the two pensions received by him equal to the pension he would have been awarded in respect to such disability, had he been serving in the military ^ service of Canada.
9.	That when a person in any of !His Majesty's naval, military or air forces other than the naval, military or air forces of Canada or in the naval, military or air forces of one of His Majesty's Allies, who was domiciled and resident in Canada at the beginning of the war has died during the war or thereafter as the result of a disability incurred during the war or demobilization, and his widow or children

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: have ibeen awarded a smaller pension than they *would have been entitled to under this proposed Act in respect of his death, such widow and such children if they were domiciled and resident in Canada at the beginning of the war, shall be entitled during the continuance of their residence in Canada to such additional pension as will make the total of the two pensions received by them equal to the pension that would have been awarded if the person aforesaid had died in the military service of Canada.

The resolution now before the committee is to give effect to the report of the Committee on Pensions which has been considering this matter ever since the House opened, and upon this report the Government will introduce the Bill which that committee has already prepared and reported to the House.
Have you not already a Pensions Board?
This is to give it statutory authority.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has a report of that committee been submitted to the House?

Yes, it was submitted this morning. The Government now is submitting this resolution in the terms of the report of the committee, and proposes to introduce the identical Bill which the committee has already reported to the House. The members of this committee will be interested to know-and I mention it as indicating the consideration which the Pensions Committee has given to this matter

that twenty-nine meetings were held to consider the various aspects of this pension problem, and at least three sub-committees investigated particular phases of the question. The conclusions which are embodied in the report of the committee represent the mature judgment of its members. I cannot say that all the clauses of the Bill and all the conclusions in the report were agreed to by every member, but I can say that the majority of them were accepted unanimously, and where that was not the case the great majority of the committee were in favour of the conclusions reached. So that we have before us the considered conclusions of a very large and responsible committee of the House.
My hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has asked if we have not already a Board of Pensions Commissioners. Yes, we have. The House will no doubt be interested in a brief statement of the legislation relating to pensions for our overseas military forces-. The first provision made for such pensions was by two Orders in Council of the 29th of April, 1915. These orders provided for the payment of $264

per annum for total disability for the rank and file, and a similar amount for widows or dependent widowed toothers -of those killed, and a scale of four degrees of disability. If hon. members are interested in the full Teport of the committee they will find it in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings at page 431 and subsequent pages. That was the situation when the House met in the early part of 1916. A committee was then appointed to 'take into consideration this whole matter of pensions to dependents and to disabled soldiers. That Committee, after very careful consideration, recommended a substantial increase, and the Government, by Order in Council, gave effect to the recommendation. That Order, passed on the 3rd of June, 1916, increased the total disability pensions for the rank and file from $264 to $480, and to $382 for widows and dependent widowed mothers, and the scale of disability was extended from four to six degrees. The provision made by that Order in Council continued in force during 1916 and the greater part of 1917, but owing to the increasing cost of living, which became very manifest in 1917, and the representations
5 p.m. which were made to the Government that the existing scale was inadequate, the pensions were increased approximately 25 pet cent by Order in Council of 22nd of October, 1917. The increases were from $480 to $600 per annum for total disability, and from $382 ito $480 per annum for widows and dependent parents, and the scale of disability was extended from six to twenty degrees. This increased scale went into effect as from the 1st of April, 1917, and was in force when the House met last year.
The Committee of last year gave consideration not only to the amount that we should pay by way of pensions, but also to the pension legislation embodied in the existing, Orders in Council, and its report to this House was accepted and subsequently given effect to by the Government by an Order in Council, passed in. December, 1918. When the pension schedules were before the Committee last year they considered that the existing scale was as large as they were justified in recommending to the House. It appeared from the evidence given before the Committee last year that our then scale of pensions was higher than that in any of the other countries at war- that Canada was at the top of the list in providing pensions for dependents of those who had fallen in battle and for those who had been disabled in the service of their

country. During the year, however, it was strongly represented to the Government that in the case of pensioners with families the allowance for children was not adequate, nor was it adequate in the case of orphan children. Therefore by Order in Council in January last an addition was made to the amount allowed for children of pensioners and for orphan children. That was the situation when the matter came before the Pensions Committee for consideration this year. The Committee heard many witnesses and received representations from the Great War Veterans' Association and other organizations interested in returned soldiers-patriotic societies, boards of trade, and all classes who desired to appear and state their views with reference to the scale of pensions. They also had communications from various organizations and from many individual pensioners and thleix [friends. All these representations were carefully considered by the Committee. The result is embodied in the report of the Committee and in the resolution now before the House.
At present our whole pension legislation is embodied in Orders in Council which have been passed during the war under the War Measures Act. No doubt there was advantage in having the legislation in such form that it could be readily changed to meet changed conditions, but the time has come when, in the judgment of the committee-and the Government concurs in the conclusion-this legislation should be embodied in a statute which will not be open to change except by the Parliament of Canada. We already 'have the Board of Pension Commissioners, which was established to administer the existing pension law as embodied in these Orders in Council. The object of the Bill which will be based upon this resolution is to create this body as a statutory body, to put into statutory form the existing regulations, and to set forth in that statute the scale of pensions now recommended by the committee.
When the committee came to consider the existing scale of pensions this year they decided that certain changes should be made. Under the schedule now in force, which may be found in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday, hon. members will see that the allowance for total disability is $600, for a private and corporal in the militia, and for all ratings below petty officer in the Naval Service. Under the regulations as they stood prior to this report, a married man without children received an additional allowance of $96. It was the view of the Pensions Committee that
that was not a sufficient additional sum to allow in the case of a married man, and they recommend that the amount be permanently increased from $96 to $180 a year, which is an increase from $8 to $15 per month.
Another permanent increase which the committee felt should be made was in the case of the eldest child of a widowed mother; widowed mothers have found it exceedingly difficult to get along under the existing scale of pensions. We decided that the existing pension with respect to the eldest child was not adequate and we propose to increase it from $12 to $15 a month, or from $144 to $180 a year. Then, we have recognized in the past that an orphan child stands in an exceptional position, and it was considered that there should be an increased allowance in that case also. We have in the past provided that the allowance for the first orphan child should be double that for the first child of a widow. We continue that provision, and thus increase that allowance from $288 to $360 in the case of the orphan child. These increases affect all ranks; there is equality of pensions so far as it relates to the allowances for the wife and for children of the men of all ranks.
The committee felt that owing to the present abnormal cost of living some additional provision should be made in respect of the regular pension. They did not feel justified in recommending a permanent increase, because our pensions are already higher than those in force in any other country. They recommend that for this year a war bonus be granted to certain classes of pensioners. They propose a bonus of 20 per cent to men suffering total disability, increasing the amount from $600 to $720. The bonus also applies to all suffering a lesser degree of disability; it is scaled down in proportion. Then, it is proposed that the widow's pension, which is now $40 a month, shall be increased by a war bonus of 20 per cent, making it $48 a month. If she has one child, thus entitling her to an additional $15, the amount is * brought up to $63 a month, as compared with $52 per month under the present regulations.
The committee recommend also that where a man is totally incapacitated there should be an increase in the allowance which may be granted by the Board of Pension Commissioners to that man for personal care. Members of the committee will realize that there is a difference between total disability and total incapacity; a man may be totally disabled, according

to the pension regulations, but still be capable of earning something, and the regulations provide that in that case such earnings shall not be deducted from the pension. For instance, a man who loses both legs is considered as totally disabled; but we can understand how a man in that condition might be able to earn, in certain occupations, a substantial sum in addition to his pension. So that total disability does not imply absolute helplessness. Now, if the man is helpless, the existing regulations provide that he may be given an additional allowance of $300; the committee recommend that that be increased to $450. Thus a helpless man, suffering total disability, might receive, under the new regulations, $720, including the war bonus in respect of total disability, and, in addition, $450 in respect of his helplessness, or a total of $1,170. If he were a married man he might receive $180 more, which would be $1,300, with any further allowances, of course, in respect of children, on the scale provided.
Hon. members will see that there is a very substantial advance upon existing pension provisions, and it indicates the view of the committee as to what should be done for our Canadian soldiers. One of the results of this advance to privates is that we brought their pension up to a standard which is higher than that of the non-commissioned officers. We, therefore, purpose raising the pensions of non-commissioned officers up to a standard which will make them equal to the increased pensions of the privates. I am sure the members of the committee will agree that the members of the Pensions Committee were right in doing so, and that explains other increases in the pension schedule. It was absolutely necessary and only fair to bring the pensions of a non-commissioned officer up to that of a private, so that we have equality of pensions to that extent. The changes I have briefly outlined are the changes in the pension schedules for those who now come under our pension regulations. As the law now stands we take the income or earnings of a -widowed mother into consideration in fixing the amount of her pension. If a widowed mother is earning $20 per month, the Board of Pension Commissioners would allow her only $20 a month in order to bring her income up to $40 a month, the reason being that $40 per month is the basis upon which the pension is granted, it being the estimate of the amount required to maintain a woman under the conditions provided in the pension regulations. The committee

reached the conclusion that that was not fair to the widowed mother; that if she was able by her own effort, energy and ability to supplement her pension by her own earnings we should not deduct her earnings from the amount of her pension. Therefore, the new legislation provides that the personal earnings of a widowed mother shall not be deducted nor considered in awarding the amount of the pension. That is one important change.	,
No matter what the amount of her earnings?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No matter what the amount of her earnings. Certain municipalities in Canada have effected insurance upon the lives of soldiers living in those municipalities who went overseas. Under the existing regulations, the Board of Pension Commissioners felt themselves compelled-and I have no doubt they were rightly interpreting the regulations-to take into consideration, in awarding a pension to the dependent mother or father or brother or sister of a soldier not only their income and their ability to support themselves, but the amount of the pension received on the life of the soldier who was killed in action. You will recognize there is a clear distinction between a pension granted to a widow in respect of the death of the husband and a pension granted to a father or mother in respect of a child. In the case of the pension granted to a widow in respect of the husband, the pension is absolute, no matter what the financial condition of the widow may be, because it was the duty of the husband to support her, and the State, recognizing that fact, grants the pension regardless of her financial position. But when you come to pensions for dependent parents or dependent brothers and sisters, the pension is granted only in case the parents or other relatives are in a dependent condition and would be dependent upon those children for support, and there was reasonable ground for believing that the children would be contributing to their * support. In that case the financial position of the parents must necessarily be taken into account. In considering the matter from that standpoint, the board felt that they must take into account the amount of the life insurance placed upon the life of the soldier by the municipal corporation which insured his life and which is paying the insurance to the parents, in many cases, at the rate of so much a month. The committee reached the conclusion that that was not right; that if a

municipal concern undertook to effect insurance upon the life of a soldier for the benefit of the parents, the Dominion Government should not, so to speak, apply that on account of the pension which we should pay. We, therefore, provide that the insurance money paid under a municipal insurance of the kind I have described shall not be taken into account in awarding a pension.

Why should that not
apply to all insurance effected upon the life of a soldier?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The committee did not
consider themselves justified in extending it beyond the limit I have mentioned. That, of course, can all be discussed when we get into committee on the Bill.
In addition to the changes I have mentioned, the Committee has recommended some other very important changes, and I want to mention them now so that the Committee will have time to consider them before the Bill comes into Committee. We had strong representations made to us that Canadians or any men domiciled in Canada, who enlisted and fought in any branch of the Imperial service and who returned to Canada to reside, should be entitled to the same treatment as Canadians serving in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. There are many different classes that come under that general description. The claims of the Canadians who served in the Royal Air Force have been strongly presented to us. Until the last month or two of the .war we did not have a Canadian Air Force, and our Canadians, therefore, were encouraged to enlist in the Imperial Air Forces, where they fought so magnificently in the cause for which our Canadians were fighting. It was represented to us that it was not fair to those Canadians who fought in the Royal Air Force to come back here and receive a smaller pension than our Canadian boys who fought in our infantry, cavalry or any other branch of our service. Many Canadians, with the approval of the Government of Canada, enlisted in the Imperial Motor Transport Service and other branches of the Imperial 'Service. We had also the case of British reservists who were residing in Canada, and were called out at the opening of the war and who fought overseas. Many were killed in action, their dependents still live in Canada; others were wounded and have returned to Canada to reside. The Committee gave this matter a great deal of consideration, and they reached the conclusion that, on the whole,
the fair and right thing to do was to supplement the disability pensions of all our citizens who fought in any branch of the Imperial Service, and who have returned to Canada so long as they remain in. Canada, and of the dependents of those who have fallen, so long as these dependents remain in Canada, by a sum sufficient, together with the pension granted by the Imperial Government, to bring their pensions up to those paid to disabled members or dependents of members of our Canadian forces.
Does that apply also to French reservists who were in Canada and who served in the French army?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am just coming to that. .Then the committee had presented to them the question which the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has raised. After giving that matter very careful consideration-of course, we could not deal with one of our Allies on a different basis from the rest-the committee reached the conclusion that in the case of widows or orphan children of any of our Allied reservists who were domiciled in Canada before the war broke out and who are now domiciled in Canada, their pension shall be supplemented so long as they remain in Canada, so as to bring it up to the scale of our Canadian pensions for widows and orphans. All our Allies are put on the same basis in that respect.	'

Will that apply to the men themselves? In the case of a man, for instance, domiciled in Canada who served in the French army and lost a hand, would the very small pension he would receive from the French Government be supplemented?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The committee decided no in that case. The committee thought they had gone as far as they were justified when they decided to supplement the pensions of all who had fought in the Imperial forces, for it was the same army as the Canadian army. The committee thought that if they made provision for the widows and orphans of the Allied reservists they would be doing the fair thing. The French pensions, I might say, have recently been substantially increased, so that a French reservist residing in Canada now receives in case of total disability a pension of $480 a year. A revision of the French pension law took place either the latter part of last year or the first part of this.	.

Mr. MdMASTER: That would make it all the cheaper for us to do justice.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: I have set forth in general outline the result of the committee's deliberations. They have made some important modifications in the regulations, and these will come up when we consider the Bill clause by clause. What I thought of suggesting to my hon. friend was this: In view of the fact that this whole matter has received such full consideration by a committee of the House composed of members from both sides, and as this resolution, simply carries out the report of the committee, which has already been approved by the House, could we not permit this resolution to pass, upon which I would at once introduce a Bill so that it may he printed and placed in the hands of the members at the earliest possible opportunity. Then when the Bill comes up, the whole matter could be further discussed. I shall be glad to answer any questions hon. members desire to ask.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: I see no objection to the course proposed. It would be advancing the Bill a stage, and any discussion that could take place on this resolution can be had on the Bill.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: I have in mind a concrete case that I presented before the committee, and which I have not heard the minister deal with, although I may have missed it. It is the case of a widow whose eldest son, her main support, was killed at the front. Her husband who was the clergyman of one of our leading churches, died while the son was overseas so this woman was robbed of both her husband and son. The Pensions Board almost immediately granted the (widow a pension of $480 on account of the loss of her son. Finding out .a little later that she was receiving from a church pension fund the sum of $300, which her husband had earned by reason of being a clergyman for many years, and which was a right coming to her outside of the war, the Pensions Board deducted $300 from the $480 'and placed the widow on their pension list for only $180. That seems to me .a great injustice, 'and I should like to hear whether the board have power to deduct this $300 which the widow was justly entitled to.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
The question was con-
' sidered at great length by the Committee as to whether income-I am not speaking now of earnings-which a widow might receive from any source, should be deducted in awarding a pension. While there is a great deal to be said in favour of my hon. friend's view, the judgment of the Committee was that they would be depart-
256 i
ing from the principle upon which pensions are granted to parents if they took into consideration income that was not earned. Therefore the hon. member's suggestion is not embodied in the Bill. When the Bill comes up and we are considering the clauses which deal with this matter the hon. member's suggestion may be further considered.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
I would like to draw the minister's attention to an anomaly under the old regulation whereby, if a widow entitled to a pension was working, the amount she earned would be deducted from the pension. To illustrate my point, let me give a concrete case. A widow in Montreal had two sons and one daughter; her sons were earning pretty good salaries and were taking care of her. They both went to the front and were killed, and the widow was granted a pension of $80 a month. Finding that this was not sufficient to keep her daughter and herself she secured a position at $70 a month. Only the other day she received a letter dated June 21, which I will read to the House:
Madam,-I have the honour to inform you that in accordance with recent legislation passed by the Government your award of pension has been reduced to $10 a month.
This reduction will be effective from next *payment.
Tour obedient servant,
The Secretary,
Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada,
Per M.S.
So that she would get the same amount if she were not working. This is utterly unjust. If this woman has the energy and courage to earn some more money she should be entitled to her whole pension. I was glad to hear the minister state that under this Bill the amount of her earnings would not be deducted. I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister for the reason that the date of this letter is the 21st June and it states that the decision is according to recent legislation. Another reason why I bring this matter up is that the report of the committee, as contained in the Votes and Proceedings of yesterday, does not specify this change in the legislation. I hope that in the interval this will be incorporated in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
The report presented to
the House yesterday was accompanied by the Bill and the Bill does contain a provision to meet the case that my hon. friend has referred to.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: When will it be distributed? It is not printed yet.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
It will be available foi
distribution as soon as it is formally introduced and printed, and that is why I am anxious to get the resolution through.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: It is well understood that a provision will be enacted in the Bill which will prevent the deduction of earnings from the pension?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
That is in the Bill that the Government intend to introduce.
/Mr. McMASTER:	Mr. Chairman, I am
well aware of the difficulty that anybody who drafts a pension law encounters in the effort to do justice to the recipient of the pension and still deal fairly and reasonably yith the taxpayers. But I must say that I would like to see the Government go a little farther with regard to those men who are naturalized citizens of 'Canada and who, at the outbreak of the war, went to their respective armies and fought in the cause of freedom and of the Allies. The matter comes home to me because of a striking incident that occurred in a town in the county which I have the honour to represent. There was a Frenchman who came and settled in this country and was naturalized as early as 1900. He was a skilful military man, having spent eight years in the French army. At the outbreak of the war he was anxious to join the Canadian army, but the French consul in Montreal instructed him that it was his legal and, I presume moral, duty to join the army of France. By the end of August he was in France. On arrival there he was not able to join the regiment to which he belonged. He was placed with some 70,000 other men in taxi-cabs, omnibuses and other means of conveyance and sent by the military governor of Paris to take part in the great drive against the German army in the early days of 1914. He took part in the victorious battle of the Marne. After that, although a man of ovej: forty, he fought with a regiment composed of young men for three months. He was then on duty of a most dangerous character with his own regiment for months, after which he was employed guarding the lines of communication in the rear. While he was watching a line of railway, a bomb was thrown from an aeroplane near the railway track along which a trainload of British soldiers was coming. He ran to the bomb, which was on the point of bursting, picked it up, carried it for some yards and, just as it exploded, threw it away. He was injured about the face and the great part of both hands was blown away. IHe comes back to

Canada where his family have resided for many years. He is a naturalized citizen of Canada. He will not receive from the French Government the same pension, or nearly the same pension, as if he had been allowed, as he desired in the first place, to join the Canadian army.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: What is the name of that hero?

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: That hero's name is Julien Grandjean and he lives in Sutton, in the county of Brome, province of Quebec. I think a man of that calibre should enjoy the same rights and benefits of Canadian citizenship as the man who was born in Canada and who was able to enlist in the Canadian army. I would press upon the Government the justice of treating this man and other men of the same class with the same generosity that we have treated our own native-born Canadian citizens.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman investigated that story to satisfy himself that it is a mechanical possibility for an aeroplane bomb to lie around and wait to be picked up and to be carried off? A bomb thrown from an aeroplane would penetrate the ground for several feet so that even if it did fail to explode a man would be unable to get it out. The probability is that it was not an aeroplane bomb at all. I think that before you base an argument upon an incident of that kind it would be well to investigate and make perfectly sure that it is a true story.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: I have not the technical knowledge of the hon. and gallant gentleman, who has just spoken, but I can say that the facts in regard to this matter were given to me by a man whom I believe to be an honest and truthful man. I believe the story to be true.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: The truth of the story has no bearing on the matter at all; it is the principle that is at stake. It does not matter how he was injured so long as he was injured.

maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext: I have seen his hands myself. On one hand he has the little finger and thumb left and on the other he has the little finger, the ring finger and thumb left.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LAW ON MILITARY PENSIONS.-RATE OF PENSIONS.
speechtext:
I am sure we will all agree with the hon. member for Brome in appreciation of the splendid heroism of a man who has served his country, France, and his country, Canada, in the way that my hon. friend has mentioned. We cannot

speak too strongly of the courage, patriotism and self-sacrifice of the French forces. The difficulty lies in the fact that the law of France does not permit a man to part with his nationality, and he is therefore, on the outbreak of war, called up for service. My hon. friend will agree that, much as one might like to deal with cases such as he has mentioned, we cannot deal with them unless we treat all Allied soldiers on the same basis. Let me point out that the increase in our Pension Bill made in the fall of last year in increased allowances to children, plus the increases which we are now recommending, total an amount of nearly $8,000,000 a year. This is a very large additional charge upon the revenues of this country. The committee gave the class of cases that my hon. friend has mentioned very careful consideration, but we reached the conclusion that we were not justified in going farther than we have gone.
Resolution reported.
