speakerposition: topic
maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the motion that the House do now go into Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before going into Supply, I wish to bring before the House a matter of very great importance to the constituency which I have the honour of representing, and to the country generally. I refer to the removal of sand and gravel by American and Canadian companies from the west end of Lake Erie in the vicinity of Pelee island and Point Pelee, which is causing extreme erosion oi the shores of the island and also the point, carrying away the natural protection and threatening the destruction of both the island and the point. Notwithstanding that petitions from the municipality and from private parties have been sent in to the Government during a period extending back over four or five years, yet this nuisance is going on unabated.
In the first place let me give some idea of the location of this island and this point. Pelee island is not only the most southern point of South Essex, but also the southernmost point of the Dominion of Canada, situated about thirty miles southeast of
the mouth of the Detroit river and about sixteen miles from the mainland of Canada. Formed in the course of ages by a small upheaval of rock and by the rich alluvial deposits brought down by the swirling waters of the Great Lakes as they turn their course eastward towards the Gulf oi St. Lawrence, it is one of the few places in Canada which can boast of prehistoric habitation. In ancient days the Mound Builders reared on it their structures foi defence, for memorials to their dead, and for worship. It is now the peaceful abode of eight hundred patriotic and loyal British subjects. It has an area of sixteen square miles and consists of about ten thousand acres of the most fertile soil in the Dominion of Canada, of which 9,800 acres are under cultivation. For many years it was renowned for its great harvest of grapes and the excellent native wine produced from them. It is now particularly noted for its enormous crops of fall wheat, corn and tobacco. The excise revenue collected on tobacco from Pelee island alone amounts to over $100,000 per annum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
Is it good tobacco?
Mr. BRIEN. Everybody uses it. Of the total acreage under cultivation, 3,600 acres consist of excellent clay land at a higher level than the lake, and the balance of 6,200 acres have been reclaimed from the marshes, which are at a lower level than the lake, at a cost of $200,000. The drainage of this reclaimed land is carried on by means of dredge cuts or canals of a width of 35 feet, and a depth of about 8 feet, and aggregating in length about 22 miles. The water is carried from these canals into the lake by means of pumping stations, of which there are five. Point Pelee, on the other hand, is the extreme southern point of the mainland of Canada. It runs out into the lake for a distance of about nine miles from the main shore, and is formed in a similar way to Pelee Island, consisting oi alluvial soil at the extreme point, and ol decayed vegetation at the base. Nature has thrown her protecting arms about both the island and the point in the form of embankments of sand and gravel which rise to a considerable height above the high-water level and slope off into the lake to a distance of from one hundred to one hundred' and fifty yards in places, and in other places to a mile and a mile and a half, and even two miles. The current of the Detroit river divides at the north end of the island depositing there sand and other material that may be brought down along its shores, and then converges at the south end wher#

it forms a considerable sandbar. The same condition prevails around the Point, so that two great sandbars exist, one to the south of the Island and the other to the south of the Point.
These bars contain millions of yards oi the very best sand and gravel, washed and ready for use, that can be found anywhere. These two deposits of sand and gravel have attracted the eyes of speculators for years back, with the result that leases and patents have been granted to certain parties, both Canadians and Americans. At the present time all the leases have been cancelled, but there are two patents still in force. They are for water lots on the two bars I have mentioned, which are the keys to the natural protection of both the island and the point. One of these patents is controlled by an American company and the other by a Canadian company. As a consequence millions of cubic yards of sand and gravel, during the last ten years, have been exported to the United States without this country receiving anything in return.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext: What part does the American company control?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
The American company
controls the sandbar off the Island and the Canadian company the sandbar off the Point. The method in operation is to use large steam <. barges, equipped with sandsucking apparatus, which have a capacity of from 500 to 800 cubic yards, and can be loaded in two hours. This sand and gravel is carried to the ports of Detroit, Toledo, Sandusky and Cleveland, in the United States and Windsor, Ontario. The cost of operation is about 27 cents a cubic yard and I believe the material is selling at the present time, and has been for some years, at the pmds mentioned, for $1.50 to $1.80 "per cubic yard.
When we consider that millions of yards are carried away every year, some little idea can be gained of how profitable a business it is. They begin their operations at the earliest date that navigation opens and continue until the latest date in the fall. They work night and day, Sundays included. I refer now to the American companies; the Canadians are not allowed to work on Sundays. The profit from the business in which these sandsuckers, as they are commonly known down there, are engaged is about 600 per cent on the actual cost. And, let me repeat, this country is getting nothing in return.
The result is that the sandbar to the south of the Island has almost vanished. From a

quarter of a mile to half a mile of the southern part of the Island has disappeared, and the sloping breakwaters that protected both the Island and the Point at all times have also disappeared, and to-day in many places the sand embankments have given way and the water has swept in on the reclaimed lands; also the greater part of the sandbar to the south of Point Pelee and at least a quarter of a mile of the Point itself, which was originally well timbered, have been carried away.
On April 28 last I received a telegram from Mr. F. C. Barnes, a member of the Municipal Council of Pelee Island, as follows;
Lake has broken into marsh in several places through loss of natural protection hy the removal of sand and gravel.
un May 6 I received the following letter from him:
Received your letter in reply to telegram that I sent you and am pleased to see that you are taking much interest in our troubles. Mr. Brien, if,something is not done, and done quick, our island will be gone, as the sand and natural protections are mostly all gone and the waves are cutting the shores all to pieces and breaking through in several places to which we have to put logs, stones and anything we can get to save the marsh lands from flooding, and if said lands flood, the island is surely gone, as you understand the value of our rich fertile soil in the marsh which is about one-half of the island. Now, Mr. Brien, I feel assured, and I am satisfied that the rest of the council do, that you are doing all you can in our behalf. But have we got to be wiped off the map simply to fill some American people's pockets? Are we not British subjects and our island British territory? I feel assured that there is a way. If the Government will not stop it outright, why cannot there be an export duty put on so high that it will be impossible for them to take it away? As it is, our island is going and no one, not even the Government, is receiving anything except the American people. How long would Canadians go into American waters and take sand and gravel? Might also say that the United States Government will not allow sand and gravel to be taken only in harbours and such places, which saves dredging operation for their Government. If our Government could only see and understand things as we do and as they really are, surely they would stop operations at once, as there are about 800 good British subjects on this island that must sooner or later lose their homes and all. It is a very serious matter. As to operations on Fishing Point, they have been busy night and day since about March 2iSth, and also Sundays. This is another matter that should be taken up, this Sunday work. Our Canadian boats cannot load or unload on Sunday, but those sandsuckers have been working every Sunday as much as week days. Will you kindly let us know if they can operate on the Sabbath day?
At six o'clock the House took recess.

After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at 6 o'clock, I was reading a letter from a member of the Municipal Council of Pelee island setting forth the tremendous amount of erosion that was taking place on the shores of Pelee island and the great destruction of property resulting. I have also a letter which was addressed to me on June 7 last by a man who is very much interested in Point Pelee. It says:	.
Dear Sir,-I want to advise you that the sand-suckers are having a fine time. They come and go at their own sweet will, and seem to have received no instructions to the contrary. The laxity of the Government in this matter is going to drive the .people into revolution, because it means to the people interested in Point Pelee lands a loss of a great many thousands of dollars, and it will not be very long before this loss or damage will be sustained by them. I am interested to a very large sum, and I must confess that I feel that almost any proceedings will be justified in defence of our property, and if the Government who are elected to look after the interests of the people will not do so, why should the people not take the law into their own hands? This "passing the buck" by the Dominion Government over to the provincial and by the provincial piass-ing it back to the Dominion is so apparently a design on their part to avoid taking action that we are led to no other conclusion than that they are influenced to take no action.
I wish to state here that the Federal Government is interested in Point Pelee to the extent of having established there a national park or bird sanctuary. I have here a letter from the superintendent of that park, which reads as follows:
Dear .Sir.-Sandsuckers were operating all last week, close in to the end of the land at Point Pelee, two and three in number. Those cargoes are lifted in three hours' time and comprise approximately seventy-five carloads of gravel. The outer line of bars are now all gone and these vandals are steadily creeping head on to the land's end. The first mate of one of these ponderous crafts landed at the Point last week and openly boasted of the continuation that would last all the summer of 11919. The action of the lake's currents here conveys the gravel and sand from both sides of the Point to less than three-quarters of a mile out from the terminal. The operations last season have proven disastrous to the Point, jeopardizing its safety and the continuation this season will certainly ruin and wreck this old historic landmark. All this gravel is going to the United States ports and the people are swearing vengeance here. The shores on both sides of the Point north of Point Pelee are already barren of sand and gravel, and it does appear that our Government has given little heed to our people that esteem this place as a heritage. I presume it will not be necessary to report further in this transaction.
P. H. Conover.
Repeated protests have been made to the Government since 1914 against the carrying on of these operations. On February 28, 1914, a petition signed by about one hundred ratepayers of Pelee island was addressed to the reeve and councillors of the municipality of Pelee, and through them sent to the Acting Premier and other members of the Government of Ontario. The petition set forth:
1.	The importance of the island by reason of its large production.
2.	The large expenditure of the municipality to bring the marsh lands to a very high state of .cultivation.
3.	The great erosion of the shores imperilling the extensive drainage systems constructed.
4.	The cause of the increased erosion has been tremendously increased by the removal of sand and gravel from the shores and beaches of the island.
5.	The effect of the holes and depressions made by the removal of the sand and gravel is to cause the erosion of the shores to he brought down by the action of wind and water to fill these depressions.
6.	The necessity of speedy action by the Government of the province of Ontario, or incalculable injury would be done to the island and the drainage system thereon.
Following this petition, a large deputation from Pelee island waited upon the Minister of Lands, Forests and Mines, who issued instructions on March 9, 1914, for an examination of the matters complained of 'by their representatives. A report was made to the Minister of Lands, Forests and Mines by James Hutoheon, engineer of ihat department, on May 2, 1914, wherein he refers to the serious erosion of the shores, especially on the west side south of the west dock; that the gravel beach claimed by the first owners as having protected this west shore was not then in existence; that the old road on the west shore was entirely cut away, and that the stone-filled timber cribs which were built for shore protection in 1907 were now 50 feet out in the lake, which was the amount of erosion in seven years. IHle also states that north of the west dock on the west .side there was a good gravel Ibeaoh and little or no erosion. (This beach has all disappeared since then.) He also stated that the erosion of the shore at the points indicated was a serious matter to the municipality, and that adequate shore protection at that time was beyond the means of the municipality, and also that the safety of the drainage work was not seriously affected as the erosion

was going on at points where the land was high and not at that time along the drainage embankments. I may say that since that time, which means within five years, the erosion has carried away nearly all the sand embankments protecting the drainage area, and the water now in almost any storm is breaking over into the reclaimed land. The embankments have given way; no sand and gravel are to be found at that particular place.
The understanding is that the 'Government engineers at different times have reported to the departments of both the local and the Federal Governments that the removal of the sand was not causing any greater than natural erosion. As evidence of this, I submit the following letter received by me from Mr. K. M. Cameron, assistant chief engineer, Department of Public Works, Ottawa, under date of March 26th, 1919:
Tour letter of the 24th instant to the department concerning sand and gravel operations off Point Pelee, Ontario, has been referred to me as I was directly charged during the past season with the examination into this matter. A. very extensive examination was made and I beg to state that it is believed the continuance of the dredging under the regulations as laid down last season will not he a factor in the erosion of Point Pelee. The erosion which is going on, and which has been going on for a very 'great number of years, is entirely a natural one. I have recommended that our observations be continued for a further season and that dredging be allowed under the regulations as laid down last year. If, as a result of our further observations, we find it necessary to further restrict or discontinue dredging operations altogether, the matter will then be referred to the Department of Justice for atten-tton-	(Bgd.) K. M. Cameron.
On April 10, 1918, Mr. J. L. Morris, civil engineer of Pembroke, Ontario, in company with Mr. James Hutcheon, engineer for the Department of Lands, Forests and Mines of Ontario, went to Pelee island and made a very thorough examination and investigation of conditions as they then existed. The substance of his report was that there had been no great erosion of the shores of the island previous to the excessive removal of sand, but that in recent years the erosion on certain parts of the island has been at the rate of about ten feet per annum. He stated that in front of lot 30, judging by the municipal plan made by Mr. Alex. Baird, C.E., of Leamington, Ontario, in 1912, there has been an erosion of more than 100 feet, which erosion occurred between the years 1912 and 1918; and judging from data compiled by Engineer Hutcheon in 1916 and comparing with conditions as he found them in 1918, 105 feet of Fishing point, at the south end of the island, covered with

timber, had been washed away during the two seasons, and from the east side of the point 100 feet of timbered land had been washed away. At this time there was no sandbar to the south of the island. He also stated that Mr. Guy (McCormick, an old resident of Pelee island, had related to him that within his recollection the sandbar from Fishing point reached from the timber growth out into the lake one and a half miles towards Middle island, and that with the exception of a narrow channel through the sandbar he could walk from Fishing Point to the end of the bar, a distance of one and a half miles out in the lake.
He stated that during the season of 1913, 1,930 boat loads of sand and gravel were removed from around the south end of the island, and that during the season of 1917 they had reported taking 1,872 loads. As these loads average 500 cubic yards each, and as no record can be got of the total amount removed, as they work at night as well as during the day, it is a safe estimate to state that millions of yards of gravel were removed every year from in and around this vicinity. I wish also to state that this is only one company which is operating off the south end of the island, while another company is operating off the south end of the Point Pelee bar, carrying away sand, which company has fully as many boats and is working just as constantly as the other. These engineers, while claiming that damage was done, seem to recommend the building of protecting groins, etc., in order to protect the shores, instead of recommending the removal of the cause. In fact, the general opinion is that the departmental engineers advise their departments that the removal of the sand is not the direct cause of the excessive damage that is being done to both the island and the point.
On December 4, 1917, the council of the county of Essex, in session assembled, passed a resolution, copies of which were forwarded to the Minister of Lands, Forests and Mines of Ontario, and to the local representatives of North and South Essex. It set forth the great danger to Pelee island owing to the action of the sandsuckers in removing sand and gravel from the bar projecting from Fishing point, and asked that there shall be no further continuance of licenses granted by the province of Ontario to companies to remove sand or gravel from the waters of lake Erie, and that any such rights he cancelled at once and thus prevent any further destruction of Pelee island. It is inferred from this resolution that the County Council of Essex

believes that the excavation outside of Fishing point was wholly responsible for the increased erosion of the banks of Pelee island. It- is also the opinion of all local engineers, as well as of every individual who has witnessed the destruction going on, that the removal of the sand is totally responsible for the destruction that has occurred. Appeals have been made to the Ontario Government, and also to the Dominion Government, at different times, not only through representatives and solicitors, but through deputations from both Pelee island and the mainland, and at all times the answer received was that their engineers' reports were to the effect that the removal of the sand and gravel was not the cause of the excessive erosion going on, but that it was due wholly to natural causes.
In the meantime, however, all leases have been cancelled, and to-day there remain the two patented water lots, one of which- namely, the one at the south end of Pelee island-is owned and controlled by an American company known as the Sandusky Sand Company, managed by a firm called Homegardner & Hendrickson. This lot is partly land above water and partly under water. The other is on the bar projecting out from Point Pelee. The difficulty now seems to be that the Ontario Government cannot cancel these patents, as they are owned outright, and the only thing that can be done is for the municipality or the Government, who are being damaged, to take action through the courts to restrain further operations and to obtain redress for damages done. A letter under date of March 27, 1919, written to me by Mr. J. G. Kerr, of Chatham, Ontario, solicitor for the municipality of Pelee island, explains the position the island is in with regard to this matter, as follows:
I am writing you at the request of the council of the township of Pelee. The reeve and clerk and Mr. Barnes, one of the councillors, have been in consultation with me for some time today with regard to the litigation that the island is having with the parties who are dredging for gravel at the south of the island. I started an action for the township with the approval of the Attorney-General for Ontario about a month ago, and so that you may understand exactly what is in question, I am sending you herewith a copy of the statement of claim that has been filed and served in that action. The defendants have not yet put in their statement of defence, but from correspondence that I have had with their solicitors, it is quite plain to me now that I cannot force them to a trial this spring. The council is very much concerned about the matter. It is one of life and death in so far as Pelee island is concerned. The menace is growing and al-readv on several occasions the water has
broken over the drainage embankments and the islanders are convinced that unless they get some protection and get it shortly there is going to be some very great damage done in the near future. It is apparent to me that even if the island succeeds in the litigation it is still going to be necessary to construct some artificial protection along the shore. This has been reported on from time to time by Government engineers and township engineers, but there is a report made by the district engineer at Windsor in 1915 on file in the Public Works Department in which there are some specific recommendations by that engineer along the line of construction of groins. I think the engineer in his report goes extensively into the enormous profits that these gravel operators are making and suggests that by taxation they could be made to bear a substantial part of any expense incurred by the Government. The islanders are not inclined to concede anything to these gravel operators as they are absolutely convinced that the erosion has been very greatly increased by their operations. They have excavated a great basin to the south of the island so that now where formerly there were sand banks and accumulations of sand that were really dry land nearly the year round there is from ten to thirty feet of water. A great many acres of dry land have already been washed away and the erosion is going on at such a rate that unless something is done there is no question but what Pelee island will be in the course of a few years reduced to just those parts of the island which consist of rock formation and that would mean practically the destruction of the island. The district engineer in the report that I have mentioned strongly recommends works of protection and further points out that it is the duty of the Government to do these works. For some reason or another, the matter was not followed up in 19ft'5. But the council feels now that a determined effort ought to be made to get the Government to take some action.
There are two lines upon which the Dominion Government can act. The one would be to stop the gravel operations and the other would be to construct works of protection. I understand that the United iStates Government has put a stop long ago to all similar operations in their part of lake Erie and the council would like to press upon the Government the necessity of stopping these excavations, either by some express act of the Government or by imposing such an export tax upon gravel as to make the business unprofitable. You probably know who the men are that are conducting these operations. They are German Americans in Sandusky and they are making enormous profits, and neither the Dominion Government nor the Ontario Government nor the township of Pelee are deriving any revenue from them. They, of course, have plenty of money and will no doubt be able to get engineers to contend that the dredging operations are not the cause of the trouble. They can show, of course, that erosion is going on elsewhere but the men on the island know that since these dredging operations have assumed the large scale they have that the erosion on the island is doubling in force and in intensity. They know that since these dredging operations began all the natural protection which formerly existed has been swept away. It is almost self-evident that the construction of a huge basin at the south of the island would gather to it all the loose material from the shores of the island, the currents on both the east and west shores being from the

north to the south, so that the sand hanks that formerly existed paralleling the shores and which formerly took the most of the weight of the wave action are now gone and the waves allowed to break directly upon the shore. This is what is causing the more rapid erosion and the islanders feel that they must fight and fight to a finish and that if they cannot succeed now in getting protection and in stopping these excavations they might as well give up the idea of any permanent home or property on the island.
I wrote some days ago to the Public Works Department for a copy of the District Engineer's report and also for copies of certain other reports with regard to similar operations near Point Pelee. I would like to have these reports so that I could go over them carefully with the council, and then we would like to come to Ottawa and interview with you the Minister of Public Works and also, if possible, the Acting Premier, Sir Thomas White, so that we could discuss both the engineering problem and the question of either stopping the export of gravel from the vicinity of the island or imposing an export tax upon It.
The council tell me that you are personally familiar with the whole matter and anxious to assist them, and I therefore feel encouraged to lay the matter before you at this length. The council would like an appointment at an early date as they will soon toe very busy with their farming operations, but as their telephone cable is not working it usually takes a couple of days at least to communicate with them, so please let me know' as far ahead as possible and by telegram what date the minister fixes for the interview.	J. G. Kerr.
I wish to state here that Mr. Kerr has been only recently engaged by the municipality of Pelee island as their solicitor; they having tried many others during the past years in their attempts to get results through the process of law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext: Who has changed ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
The plaintiffs changed solicitors at different times, hoping some one else would get action more than the one they previously had. I wish to state also that, from this letter and from the engineers' reports that I have read, it seems that the engineers recommend protection in the way of groins and supports in order to protect the island from the erosion that is going on, but in no case do they strongly recommend the stopping of the cause, which is the removal of the sand.
An interview was arranged with the Minister of Public Works of the Dominion, as requested in the above letter, with the result that the department did not consider that they had any jurisdiction in this matter, as it was purely provincial. We then pointed out to the Minister of Public Works that his department was responsible for the upkeep and maintenance of a lifesaving station on Point Pelee and the lifesaving crew's lodging house on Point Pelee,

and that the same conditions prevailed here [DOT]as on the island, and that if conditions were to go on as they had been, it would only be a matter of a short time until Point Pelee would be destroyed and with it the life-saving station and lodging house. He promised to give the matter his serious consideration, and in a few days sent me the following letter, under date of April 8, 1919:
I have been giving a good deal of consideration to the subject matters presented to me by yourself and constituents one day last week re Pelee island. After having read the memoranda of the solicitors for the island very carefully, I am at a loss to see wherein the Federal Government plays any part, or is in any way responsible for the unfortunate position in which these people find themselves, because I must admit from the' statements made that there is danger of serious damage to this very valuable island. It seems that in the first place the province of Ontario granted a sand bank at the south end of the island to one McCormick, and later on leased a very large area to the east thereof, from which different parties have taken very large quantities of gravel, and I presume the province of Ontario is receiving a royalty for the gravel taken from the leased portion of the island. The contention now is that owing to the dredging operations the sand, and gravel from further up the side of the island is being washed down to fill up the vacancy, and my judgment 'is that it would be useless to expend any money in trying to protect the banks of the island until the real cause of the difficulty is removed, that is, until the province of Ontario cancels the lease and, if necessary, by legislation takes steps to prevent any further dredging operations at the south end of the island. Even after that were done, I do not see where the Federal Govern-, would be at all responsible or perhaps even justified in expending any money to help repair the damage done along the shores of the island, but if we were sure that no further dredging was to take place wre would then be very glad indeed to consult with you and the Ontario Government as to the best means of preventing damage in the future.
F. B. Carvell.
On the same occasion, we took the matter up with the Department of the Interior. The Minister of the Interior stated that this was purely a provincial matter over which they had no jurisdiction, but when we stated that the department had established a national park or bird sanctuary on the Point and that it was threatened with destruction, he felt there was reason for complaint and promised to give the matter serious consideration, and the department has since cancelled all leases that it had granted. In a few days I received the following communication, under date of April 1, 1919:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 24th ultimo, addressed to the Minister of the Interior, in which you make inquiry regarding sandsucking operations off Point Pelee, and in reply

beg to say that the Commissioner of Dominion Parks, to whom your inquiry was referred, reports as follows:
[DOT]< i believe that the only sand and gravel leases granted by the Dominion in the vicinity of Point Pelee were those granted by the Interior some years ago for specified areas on the Point itself. Several months ago notice of cancellation of these leases was served upon the lessees. No operations have been carried on with respect to any of these leases and therefore the operations of which Dr. Brien complains are evidently the operations of dredges on water lots off the Point. I understand the dredging company which operates there has some Crown grants and also some leases from the provincial Government with respect to a number of water lots. My understanding of the situation is that the province and not the Dominion controls the land under the water and that therefore the operations which are going on are not carried on through any authority from the Dominion. The Department of Public Works is concerned in these dredging affairs in so far as they may affect navigation and associated matter. Last year, Mr. Cameron, Consulting Engineer of the Department of Public Works, and Mr. Kindle of the Geological Survey, made a general investigation with respect to the effect of the dredging .operations upon navigation and in regard to erosion along the shore. The Department of Public Works is therefore the department in the best position to advise Dr. Brien as to the present situation.
I trust this information will be satisfactory.
W. W. Cory.
We also took the matter up with the Department of Marine and Naval Service. They also claimed that they had no jurisdiction as the matter was purely provincial. We explained to them that they had three of the finest harbours in lake Erie under their control, namely, the east and west sides of Point Pelee, and the south end of Pelee island, and that if conditions went on as they were, it would only be a matter of a short time until these harbours would be completely destroyed, and we thought that it would be to their interests to assist in this serious matter. The following letter, addressed to me under date of March 25th,	1919, from the
Department of Marine, explains their attitude in the matter:
In reply to yours of the 24 th instant regarding the question of sand-sucking operations at Point Pelee, Ontario, I would say that extensive investigations in this connection have been carried out during the past season, and the opinion of the investigators appears to be that these operations have very little effect on the general erosion going on in that vicinity. At the same time, they recommend that the operations be kept within certain limits which they define, and it seems that the provincial government, which is actually in control of the situation, is willing to co-operate.
There is some doubt as to whether the regulation of this matter comes under the provisions of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, but if so, any action taken should lie within the province of the Department of Public Works
rather than the Department of Marine. This department would not, however, hesitate taking the matter up with the Department of Public Works for vigorous action should it appear at any future time that these operations are actually detrimental to navigation.
C. Stanton.
We then took it up with the Department of Justice, with the result that they stated that this was a purely provincial matter over which they had no jurisdiction.
I wrote the department asking for a copy of the engineer's reports which I knew were in their possession, and received from them the following letter under date of April 28, 1919, which explains their attitude in the matter:
Referring to your letter of the 25th instant,
I have to inform you that the reports prepared by Dr. Kindle and the engineers of the Public Works Department were prepared with a view to taking legal proceedings' against persons dredging in the neighbourhood of Point Pelee in such a manner as to cause erosion. Whether or not the dredging is the cause of the erosion has not been finally determined, the engineers desiring to make further observations during the present dredging season. Consequently I do not think it would be desirable in the public interest to make public the results of the scientific investigation made to date.
W. Stuart Edwards.
We then brought the matter to the attention of the then Acting Prime Minister, who brought the whole matter before council and reported to me that as these patents were granted by the Provincial Government, they had no jurisdiction in the matter and did not want to interfere with provincial rights.
I wish to state that at all times we have had the most courteous consideration given to our appeals by the different departments of the Dominion Government, but we feel now that the four departments which I have mentioned, namely, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Marine and Naval Service, the Department of the Interior and the Department of Justice, should be joint plaintiffs with the municipality of Pelee island, through the Department of Justice, and force ^he issuing of an injunction restraining these sand companies from further operations until the matter can be settled in the courts and the amount of damage determined.
I have also accompanied deputations from Pelee island and Point Pelee before the Department of Lands, Forests and Mines of the province of Ontario, and on each occasion they stated that the reports of their engineers were to the effect that the removal of the sand and gravel was not the direct cause of the destruction

going on at the Island and the Point. I herewith quote letters, under date of May 5, 1919, from the Department of Lands, Forests and Mines of the province of Ontario in answer to letters of inquiry, which explain their attitude in this matter:
Replying to your letter of the 29th ultimo, addressed to the Prime Minister in reference to the erosion at Point Pelee and Pelee Island, I have to advise you as follows:
There are no operations carried on in this vicinity now under authority from this department.
In July, 1897, a patent was granted to Peregrine McCormick of a water lot on Fishing Point at the southerly end of the island, and sand and gravel has been removed from this patented area over which this department has no control.
In 1913, a lease was issued for the removal of sand and gravel from the bed of the lake lying east of the water lot granted to McCormick to H. C. Hansen, of Cleveland, Ohio, but this lease has been cancelled, and as I stated before, no operations are being carried on under any authority from this department. Action has been brought by Messrs. Kerr and McNevin, Barristers of Chatham, on behalf of the township of Pelee and others to restrain the removal of sand and gravel from the water lot which was patented, and the Attorney General of this province has been connected in the case as a plaintiff. You will, therefore see that this department has not only stopped every one from removing sand and gravel over whom they have control, but also assists the municipality in their action against the owners of the patented water lot.
T. W. Gibson.
Under date of April 30, 1919, I received this letter in answer to an inquiry:
My understanding of the situation of Pelee Island was that an action was to be brought to restrain sand and gravel operators and to recover damages. This department has stopped nil operations over which it has any control. To ascertain the exact situation in connection *with the matter you would have to consult the solicitor for the parties. G. H. Ferguson.
On June 11, 1919, I received another letter as follows:
The Prime Minister referred your letter of the 6th instant to this department.
As already advised you, this department has stopped sand and gravel operations absolutely, in so far as it has any control over the situation. Of course, you will understand that the two patents which were long since issued to private parties are beyond the control of the Crown. It may ibe that the sandsuckers are operating on these areas; if so, I take it that the solicitors for the parties will advise them that they have an action for damages if injury is done by the operation of the boats. This department has done everything to the utmost limit of its powers to protect the local interests, and intends to maintain that position.
G. H. Ferguson.
From the above letters we conclude that the province of Ontario is behind the municipality of Pelee island in bringing 
action in the courts to restrain sand and gravel operators and to recover damages, yet the municipality of Pelee island appealed by petition and deputation to the Ontario Government in 1914 and several times since, .and litigation has been going on since that time. Still, in spite of all this, the sand and gravel is being removed to-day in greater quantities than ever. The general opinion is that the Ontario Government or the Federal Government can settle this matter at once if they so desire. I took a clipping from the Leamington Post which is issued in the town' closest to the scene of these operations. It reads as follows:
From one to three sandsuckers are reported to be operating daily at Point Pelee, swiftly completing tile destruction that has been going on there for years. Although assurances have been given that the Government would put an end to these operations, the promise has not been fulfilled. The only conclusion to he arrived at is that the Government is also in the grip ct the sandsuckers and afraid to act.
What I would advise is this: If there is no law on the statute-book at the present time covering this case, it is the duty of this Government to place one there at the earliest possible moment in order to control these people in their nefarious acts. The Government has a mandate from the people to do this and I do not see why they should delay any further. I think that an Order in Council might be brought down to restrain these operations. If I were to suggest the principle of the Order in Council that might be brought down, or the legislation that might be brought in, and which I believe would be passed by this House just as quickly as the amendment to the Immigration Act, which was passed in a few minutes about three weeks ago, the principle of that legislation would be something like this: Prohibition of the exportation of sand or gravel to the United States by any person or persons, from any place in the Canadian waters of lake Erie or from the islands or shores of said waters, without a special permit from the adjacent or nearest municipality from which the sand or gravel is proposed to be taken.
The people of the island have appealed in vain, they have withstood and resisted the ravages of the winds and the waves, but they are now at the mercy of these ruthless pirates. Three weeiks ago, I personally visited the scene of these ravages, .and I can testify to all that has been said. The destruction of property and the erosion of the shores are beyond description by the oasual observer. I saw where the embankments had given away in many places,

and the lake has flooded the reclaimed land. I saw where sandbags, logs, stones, etc., had been hurriedly rushed to fill up the gaps and stem the tide. I saw where a few years ago there was a beautiful sand and shingle beach sloping out for rods into the lake, now only an eroded shore dropping off suddenly into deep water. I observed that the once-beautiful sandbar which stretched from the south end of the island a mile and a half into the lake was gone, -and in its place a few rods from land were several barges loading sand from deep water. It seems to me from all these facts that this matter has not been taken seriously by those in authority.
Mr. Speaker, this is, without doubt, a most profitable business, worth millions every year to these big companies; therefore they are not going to give up easily. They are going to fight the matter to a finish. They have retained the very best counsel obtainable and the general opinion is that they gather under their subtle influence all those who might have influence against them.
The distress signals are out at Pelee island, Point Pelee, and on the shores of the mainland of South Essex. The homes and property of hundreds of our people, and two of the beauty spots of Canada are going to be wiped out unless some action is taken, and taken quickly. It is most exasperating to our Canadian people to see a portion of our country carried away to the United States, to see wanton and wholesale destruction of our property, for no other purpose whatever than to fill the coffers of the rich and satiate the greed of those who have no regard for the rights of others.
Again, I say, the air is surcharged with appeals from these patriotic British subjects. They are calling for help, and the burden of their cry is:
You take my house when you take the prop that doth sustain my house ;
You take my life when you take the means whereby I live.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of saying a few words in support of the proposition of my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Brien). He has so thoroughly covered the ground that there is little for me to say. I certainly do feel that it is up to the Government to take some action in this matter. It is an international question. When you take into consideration the fact that^ nineteen of these sandsuckers are operating in that district around Pelee island, that nine-tenths of the material is carried to the
United States and disposed of at Sandusky, Cleveland, and Detroit, and that the Dominion and the province do not receive any return whatever for this splendid material,
I am sure the House will agree that it is high time that some action should be taken. Just let me emphasize the position. Nineteen of these boats take, at the lowest possible calculation, 500 yards of gravel per load and take, as the hon. member for South Essex has stated, some two loads a day. Put it at one load, or 500 yards a day for every day, Saturday and Sunday included for eight or nine months in the year and you get this result: 500 yards equal 50 cars, or 30,000 cars per month, or 240,000 cars for the season. You have 240,000 cars of this material being carried into the United States foT the purpose of building up their industries and constructing their roads when the western part of this province is needing all its material in the worst possible way. If you lived in the western part of the peninsula of Ontario you would know that we are compelled to bring the material for road construction such as rock, a distance of 150 miles from Guelph or St. Mary's. At the same time we are allowing the very best kind of material to be carried away to the United States and disposed of there although we receive nothing in return.
We had a situation similar to this just a few years ago in the western peninsula at the point where lake Huron empties into the river St. Clair. We found that the same instruments were being used and that they were transporting tens of thousands of yards every month from the entrance to the St. Clair river and disposing of it in Detroit and other American cities. The same sandsuckers were not willing to deliver that same road-building material to the cities and towns located along the Canadian border at any kind of a reasonable figure. The outcome of it was that the Minister of Public Works of the Dominion was able to compel those boat owners to treat the Canadian people fairly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext: Was that on the occasion of the famous Sunday visit?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
This is a different proposition entirely and refers to a different part of the province. My good friend should go to Western Ontario and see beautiful Pelee island and the surrounding country, and I am sure he will fully appreciate the remarks the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brien) has made. But I want to emphasize the fact that this material is being carried off in large quantities to the United States.

Some years ago the Minister of Public Works was aible to -compel the boat owners operating on the river St. Clair to deliver similar material to the Ontario municipalities at a reasonable price. An enormous quantity of this gravel was taken from the entrance of the river St. Clair and sold in the United States. It is now delivered at a reasonable price in Canada, and roads are being built and our people served. My hon. friend has laid stress on the fact that the Public Works, Marine, and Interior Departments are vitally interested in this very .question. What I desire to urge upon the Government is the importance of taking some action, without even the lapse of another day, to prevent this valuable material from being carried away from where it is so badly needed in the western peninsula, to help build up the roads and industries of the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister ol the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-EROSION OF PELEE ISLAND AND POINT PELEE.
speechtext:
The -subject is one that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brien) has pressed with very aggressive persistency for some time, and in which, no doubt, his constituents as well as others in the district is vitally interested. Possibly the impression his address may have created that there was a disposition to shelve, or evade, the problem on the part of the Government may be best refuted if I state in my own words, and somewhat briefly, just how the question presents itself to us. The Department of the Interior is interested in that it has the ownership and administration of Pelee park which is on Point Pelee on the mainland-a stretch of territory running some nine miles southward into the lake. A portion of that is reserved as a bird sanctuary and is administered by our Parks branch. In Pelee island we have, of course, no proprietary interest. The Department of Public Works would be affected in so far as any operations interfered with navigation. The Department of Marine would be affected in so far as any operations interfered with the lighthouse stations which they maintain. The Department of the Interior would be affected should there be injury to our property, the park, by reason oi the taking away of this sand. These are the departments, and these the relative proprietary interests that are concerned in the problem at issue. I gather from the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brien), however, that he considers there is as well, on the part of the Government as a whole, a national, or, as the hon. gentleman who spoke last puts it, an international interest

in the prevention of this latest of all methods of annexing portions of our country to the United States.
Now let me discuss how far we are affected and what our duties are, I cannot speak departmentally for any except the Department of the Interior and the Department of Justice, but if I fitly represent both those departments in what I say, the House will not have very great difficulty in understanding the argument I make on behalf of the whole Government. It is quite clear no departmental action can be taken which will interfere with the progress of operations. There was a time when those engaged in this work held leases from the Department of the Interior, which leases were given on the 6th February, I think, 1913. They were brought to my attention some time last year, and, after having a report from an officer on the effect of the operations, and on examining the leases, I determined that we had a right of cancellation. My'determination on that subject was resisted by the lessees, but I exercised the right of three months' notice for which the lease provided and the resistance was not further pressed, so the leases came to an end. I understand that similar leases from the provincial government on a water lot and part of the mainland of Pelee island came to an end some time ago, and that all the operations now are conducted on two areas, one off Pelee island and one off Point Pelee, to both of which the operators have fee simple. If the committee is clear upon that point there will be little difficulty in following the rest of the argument.
Now the operators own, and they have a right to use, the property so long as they do not use it to the injury of the property of others, or to the injury of others in any respect whatever. No man can use his property in such a way as to injure another; that is a fundamental maxim of law. They cannot constitute a nuisance; they cannot interfere with navigation; and if the result of their operations is to enable the general current of the water, augmented by the effect of the winds, -to bring portions of the island to which other people have a title down into the hole created by the suction, then certainly these operators are using their property so as to injure the property of others. If what the hon. gentlemen have spoken of as, the facts are in very truth the facts, then unquestionably there is a legal right of action on the part of owners of property injured, or liable to be injured even, for damages against those operators in respect of actions already carried on, and for an injunction against fur-

ther operations. That must be fully understood before one can form a really adequate idea of what the duty of a government is. Now then, should it be that the park owned by this Dominion, and administered by the Department of the Interior, is injured or likely to be injured, it would be our duty to initiate proceedings for damages for the injuries sustained, or for an injunction to stop further injuries. The view of the Parks Branch of the Interior Department is that we have not received injury, but Mr. Harkin, the head of the branch, is apprehensive that we shall sustain some damage if these operations are further continued. Under date of June 24 he has written through the deputy minister to the Department of Justice as follows:
This department has been advised that you are taking up for the Department of Naval Service the question of the protection of their area at Point Pelee from the operations of the sandeuckers around this point.
In this connection I beg to advise you that all the Ordnance lands as shown on the plan attached have been established a Dominion park, and this department is very anxious that no sand dredging operations be allowed which will damage these lands.
They have not been damaged yet.
I should be glad if you would take whatever action is necessary in this connection.
The same or similar action would be necessary on the part of the Department of Marine if the property that they administer there, namely, the lighthouse, suffers, or is likely to suffer, damage. Those are the actions that might be taken. It appears, however, that up to date the only property injured is the property of private owners on Pelee island-private owners who hold their title from the Crown in the right of the province Of Ontario, but who own in fee simple just in the same way as the owners of the water lots. They have instituted an action in the courts of Ontario- no doubt an action for damages and for an injunction. That is the action to which my hon. friend who raises the question has referred, and that is the action in respect to which the letter was written dated 20th March, which letter stated that for some reason or other, disclosed in correspondence not read, it would be impossible to proceed this spring.
Now, even if we assume there is involved a question either national or international, it is a fundamental maxim that if the law is such that a man can protect himself before the courts of the country, then there should be no interference on the part of the Government in his behalf. Why, if a citizen
of Canada is injured in another country, the Government of Canada does not come forward on behalf of that citizen until he has failed to obtain redress in the courts of the country in which he is injured. Much more so is that the case when the courts are the courts of our own country. The courts of Canada are open to any man who may have his property injured by these operations, and, as I understand the law, if the facts' stated are established before those courts, then undoubtedly redress must follow. Because no person, however powerful or wealthy, can utilize his property to the destruction of other property.
The action has started; it has not proceeded. The progress of the action, I am afraid, we cannot assist. It is a civil action in the courts of the province of Ontario. But the province of Ontario apparently, as a Government, has seen fit to join as co-plaintiff in that action, for the reason doubtless that lands within the domain of the province are affected. It seems to me that inasmuch as those who have received the injury so far have started action, the proper course is to abide the event of that action, because it appears to be disputed that the operations on the sand are the real cause of the subsidence and the erosion of Pelee island. There does seem to be very strong reason to believe that those operations have much to do with that subsidence and erosion,-there do seem to be almost irresistible facts leading to the conclusion that it is those operations which have caused that rapid erosion in recent years. But there is no way of interfering with civil actions. And surely the citizens of our own country do not fear injustice at the hands of the courts of our own country in favour of litigants from another land. I do not think it would be fair to even intimate that such a thing was possible in the courts of Canada.
Why an application has not been made for an interim injunction, supported by affidavits of the facts as disclosed by the hon. member, I am also at a ioss te understand. In fact, his address was 9 p.m. replete with information most interesting and most useful; but where it failed in adducing facts was on the vital point,-the most vital of all- namely, why it is that the action has not been proceeded with; and, if it was impossible for the action to go to trial, why it is that proceedings were not taken to have an interim injunction in the meantime, in order that, pending the trial, no further injury might be sustained.

However, the subject is before the Department of Justice apparently from the Naval Department, and certainly from the Interior Department, with a view to considering the wisdom of our entering action similar to that entered by the proprietors of Pelee island. We, of course, could not join as co-plaintiffs, because- in this action which the municipality of Pelee island have taken we are not directly interested; we are interested in Pelee Point,- in other property altogether. We would have the right of separate action if we have sustained damage, or apprehend that we are likely to sustain damage. That point we are inquiring into now. We have not sustained damage, and we do not feel that we should have entered action before. We have submitted the question to the Department of Justice, and it is under their consideration now, as to the advisability of entering action in order to prevent injury that we fear may be sustained in the future.
Now, as to the proper position of the Government in relation to the question as an international one, I am afraid I do not fully agree with the remarks of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong). If injury is being sustained to property there is now direct recourse, and recourse that will be full and ample if the facts alleged be established. In view of that recourse being open, I do not think we ought to attempt to gain an object indirectly and circuitously when there is ample provision to gain it directly. It does not appear to me that it would be justifiable on the part of the Government or of Parliament to derogate from the title and rights of the proprietors of water lots on lake Erie, by preventing the export of sand, on the ground that that export destroys property adjoining, when the law of the land provides ample remedy in the courts for prevention of the injury and for the recovery of damages if any injury has been sustained.

I just wish to ask the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) what advice he could give us with regard to having an interim injunction against these sand operators restraining them from further action. Litigation has been going on now for sopae five years. The sandsuckers have been thwarting the law in the fact that they have been operating outside the limits which they have patented. They are also delaying the process of law in that they did not file their statement of claim in time to bring this action before the courts last spring. There is no doubt in my mind that if they lose before the courts they will appeal and get another season's operation. This is certainly a very, very serious matter. The shores of Pelee island are eroding very rapidly, and water is breaking over the dikes and flooding the reclaimed land.
The requirements of eight hundred loyal British subjects there should have immediate attention, and I again appeal to the Government to do something. Legislation should be brought down to prohibit the exportation of that sand. If we have to wait for the courts to take action in the matter, we may have to wait for years. If you take away from Pelee island and Point Pelee those two sand bars, the natural embankments and the natural protection will go also; there is no question about that.

I understand that a delegation interviewed the Government not long ago and asked that engineers who had served in the army during the war should be given some work in the field this year. Mr. McMASTElt: I see in this item a repetition of an expenditure which I challenged and criticised last session and which I see is again contained in this estimate, namely, $1,000 to the Alpine Glub. With the finances of this country in the condition in which they are at present, I cannot see

how a minister who has a feeling of public responsibility upon him can ask this committee to pay $1,000 of the people's money in order to encourage alpine climbing in the iRocky mountains. No doubt it is a very fine sport and gives to its habitues a finer idea of the beauties of nature. ,It may also possibly open up some unknown beauties of the Rocky mountains, and it may give a healthful enjoyment to the few people who are privileged to enjoy the benefits of the club, but the country's finances are in no condition to allow us to spend $1,000 of the people's money in subsidizing an alpine club, and I ask the minister to strike out this item.

I support the hon. member (Mr. McMaster) in his contention that this item should be struck out. As I understand it, people who can engage in sport of this kind are men and women of considerable wealth, many of them coming from the United States; in fact this is a rich man's sport, and I do not see why we should include in the Estimates an item of this kind. The amount is not large, it is true; it is not going to make or break the club, whether they have it or not, but it is the principle of the thing I object to, particularly at present when we are running so much behind in the finances of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the facts were as the hon. members assert, I do not think there would be any danger of the item being in the Estimates, but the facts are quite the contrary. This grant is not given by way of philanthropy, nor for commiseration, nor charity; it is given as a public investment.
What control over the expenditure does the Government retain?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just the same as in the case, I should say, of four or five hundred other expenditures of a like nature.
That is not an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The answer will come. We have no direct control, but we observe from year to year how the money is spent, and if it is spent satisfactorily, we continue it; if it is not, we do not. For example, we grant to the Forestry Association of the Dominion, I think, $4,000 a year because they carry on work which, if they did not carry it on, we would have to carry on at very much greater cost. It is a saving to the Dominion; it has been done for many years, and it will be done after the hon. member (Mr. MdMaster) gets to be a mem-

ber of the Government, if that is not too many decades ahead. There is no question about it at all, it has been done by all Governments. The Alpine Club is of value to the country in this way. The members survey the glacial and mountainous regions of this country; they publish data about them; they have associations with other clubs of a like nature and of a like class of people the world over. The circulars and literature they publish are scattered amongst all that class of people and circulate throughout the globe. As a consequence there is very considerable tourist traffic throughout our country, from which traffic Canada gets the benefit by reason of the activities of the Alpine Club. The hon. gentleman shakes his head. Is he an expert on that subject?
On mountain climbing? No.
