speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I notice that $125,000 is required to meet uncollected portion of advances of seed grain made in the western provinces by the chartered banks to holders of unpatented Dominion lands. This seems extraordinary after two or three years of good crops with prices higher than we have ever had them in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member will recall that legislation was passed in the early part of this session adopting a different method of providing seed grain. We do not provide it directly any more; we only provide indirectly for unpatented lands, that is, lands upon which are homesteaders who have not title, and therefore cannot give any security locally to the provincial or other authorities. We have to provide the seed or nobody will provide it. This is an estimate of what we may possibly be called upon to pay the banks on 1st January, I think it is, when the banks are entitled to call on us for the principal and five per cent interest in respect of any moneys they have not collected. If we have to pay this amount, or any portion of it, we take over the security, which is a lien on the land and on the future crop and so on, and we then are in the position of the banks and are entitled to collect seven per cent, so there is no possibility of this money being lost.

Is the engraving, printing and general preparation of the maps of the Dominion, for which I notice $74,375 is asked, done under contract? If so, who obtained the contract last year for the printing of these maps?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Secretary of State is not in the House. So far as the Department of the Interior is concerned, we simply requisition on the Printing Bureau and the; Printing Bureau obtain the material we requisition. Quotations are asked from the-various lithographers that are at all within, reach, including even American lithographers. Some business goes over there ; I do not know just how much.

Do I understand that this amount of $74,375 was paid last year by the department for the engraving and print-

ing of maps which were circulated by the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We pay direct to the makers of the maps, and the difference is distributed by the Printing Bureau.
I should like some of the details of the contracts given last year, or two years ago, let us say. Where are these maps printed and who printed them? Were tenders advertised for?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are rendered monthly accounts by the Printing Bureau. In my last answer I indicated that we pay the lithographers direct. We do not; we simply pay the Bureau; we have nothing to do with the original contractors at all. If the hon. gentleman would put his question on the Order Paper, he would get a complete answer.

I accept my hon. friend's word. I do not rise in any critical mood, because I generally admire these maps. If I have anything at all to say on the subject, it would simply be to caution my friend to be a little more chary about sending out these maps; many of them are useless to the parties to whom they are addressed. I receive some maps myself at times of the Northwest Territories, sections of Alberta, irrigated lands, and so on. Now, while these are no doubt exceedingly useful to parties interested in that section of the country, I think some saving might be made toy the department by taking care that the maps are sent only to those who are really interested. On the whole I am bound to say that the maps which are circulated by the department are most useful and very well got up.
Will the minister explain this item of $50,000 for the expenses of the Dominion Power Board, aud what the department purposes doing in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Dominion Power Board is constituted of the leading engineers in the services of the various departments. The chairman is Mr. Lafleur, the chief engineer of the Public Works Department.
A very able man.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not only a very able man, but a very energetic and aggressive worker. The secretary of the board is Mr. Ghallies of the Interior Department.
Is not Mr. Murphy, of the Department of Railways and Canals, a member of that board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, Mr. John Murphy.
Another able man.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. The other members ' of the board are, Mr. Stewart, of the External Affairs Department; Mr. Acres, the engineer of the Ontario Hydro-Electric; Mr. Amos, the chief water-powers engineer of the province of Quebec. Mr. Monserrat was, and I think still is, a member of the board. The duties of that board are to advise the Government on all questions relating to power development. They are engaged at present, in the main, in a study of the conditions of the St. Lawrence river, making the necessary surveys, 'Stream measurements, and so forth, to complete the surveys already made partially toy the province of Ontario and partially by the Dominion Government, in order that the imprimatur of that board may be passed upon any stand or any proposals which the Government may make with regard to power development on that river, as associated with the improvement of navigation.
This vote is to be utilized in that specific connection and it is hoped that the work that we have launched upon there will not take very long. They expect to be through with their surveys in good time to be able to advise the Government in regard to these matters. They are also advising in respect to other matters of power development in the East and in the West. The administration of our water-powers is under the Department of the Interior alone, but such water-power development is so intimately associated with navigation, shipping, and, indeed, with irrigation, that you cannot decide any problem without having those who are interested in the others taken into account. The idea of the power board is to have all interests represented. Mr. Stewart will deal with the matter from what might be called the international viewpoint. Another member of the board is Mr. Murphy, who has been with the Departs ment of Railways and Canals for a long time, and Mr. Bowden, of the same department. They will all act together and we feel that if we can in any matter get a unanimous recommendation from this body we are on pretty sound ground as regards this great question of policy connected with water-power development on the St. Lawrence river.

Does my hon. friend intend that when the power board has decided that power can be developed, say, on one section of the St. Lawrence, to lease that power to private companies, or will the

power be developed under Government control?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I certainly could not answer that question except in a general way. We are not seeking in any way, as I understand it, to develop and sell power in the province of Ontario or in any province. We cannot, however, disassociate ourselves from the great question of power development on the St. Lawrence for the reason that the St, Lawrence is a navigable stream, that you have to take navigation into account, and that navigation is a Federal responsibility alone, and, therefore, we have to interest ourselves in it. One element in the problem is to determine where the best site for the power construction is, or where the best site for the dam is, and where perhaps the second best is, because there may be one, or two, or possibly three. We must interest ourselves in that question, because a great deal depends on the kind of construction. Navigation is vitally affected not only by the nature of the power construction but also by the place at which the dam is located. That is as far as we have interested ourselves so far. When we come to the point that it is determined that a certain point is the best place for the development, then, we should take into account the provincial authority, whether it may toe Ontario or Quebec, and decide as to what shall be done with the power and just what arrangement shall be made for its distribution as it is available for use on the Canadian side.
.Mr. (OOWAN: Will the members of this board be paid for their services?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they are all members of the service and they do not get anything extra.

Is the board only temporary?
Mr. .MEIGHEN: I said they hoped not to be very long completing the necessary investigations on the St. Lawrence river. I think the board should be permanent. I see no reason to look forward to its discontinuance.

I quite agree with the minister. I think this water-power development is one of the biggest things of the future and that instead of discontinuing the board or getting the men to do the work for nothing, we should pay them all salaries, pay them well and enlarge their powers. We will have to depend very largely upon water-power in the future for industrial and other purposes.
Where will the International Dry Farming Congress, to which a grant of $3,000 is made, be held this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is usually held at Lethbridge. I imagine it will be held there this year.
I noticed that the grant was not made last year.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The congress is not held every year. I was pressed very strongly by the Government of the province to increase this grant, but I decided to keep it where it was.

Why this increase of $203,000, or forty per cent, in the vote for surveying? I understood from the minister no later than yesterday that there was no land available in Canada for settlement within the fifteen-mile belt. If the lands outside of the fifteen-mile belt are not suitable for settlement, why should we spend such a large sum for surveying Dominion lands in this country?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: During the war we steadily kept reducing the vote for surveys, lit was away over $1,000,000. The cost of surveying now is very much greater than it was before the war; consequently, relatively, we have only about half the vote here that we had at that time and at the same time the necessity for surveys is quite as great, particularly on account of the demand for soldiers' settlement. We have today a lot of work particularly for the Soldiers' Settlement Board. Of course, the survey work under Mr. Ogilvie is the basis of the permanent survey, and we have to make an advance for that this year over the previous year, although none of these amounts are within reasonable distance of what they were formerly.
I understand that all the lands within fifteen miles of a railway have been surveyed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

There are no lands within fifteen miles of a railway fit for settlement that have hot been surveyed. I understood from the minister yesterday that there were practically no lands suitable for settlement within fiteen miles. The lands, in a general way, are surveyed for a great deal more than fifteen miles from a railway. What is the purpose of increasing this amount? Why are these surveys, in a general way, being made? Because a certain amount has been spent annually for surveys, that is no rea-

son why we should continue the expenditure if it is not beneficial to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. member that we should not put money into the Estimates because it has been necessary some years before. I think we will all assume that the maximum of survey work is going on in every province. I will give the hon. gentleman a few items:
Control of field work, 1 controller of surveys and 1 inspector, $12,000.
Subdivision surveys, 18 parties, $15,000 each.
Townships have already been surveyed but they require to be divided into sections.
In which provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Eight parties are actually at work on subdivision surveys in the newer districts, and settlers are going right in, particularly soldier settlers, looking for locations. We have used surveyors, who are best qualified, to go into these districts and obtain for us a description of the character of the land, and of the general lay-out of the district, more fully than is ordinarily done in surveying, for the guidance of prospective settlers, particularly prospective soldier settlers. The demand has been very strong that we should place ourselves in the position of giving these men better information so that they will not be wasting their time, several of them running in one direction where one man going there could report whether it was worth while investigating or not. We did quite a lot of that work last year, and we will have to continue it during the coming year. Now let me read further:
Survey of lakes in Northwestern Saskatchewan of the mineral district north of The Pas and of the Manitoba-Saskatchewan boundary; one party at $210,00'0-; and one party at $25,000 $4)5,'0*00.
That is just the immediate boundary north of the old area of Manitoba. We do not intend going on to locate the country out to Hudson bay at all; we feel that that work can stand.
Surveys of water areas which are reported to have dried up; ten parties at $7,000, $70,000.
Investigation of lands for soldier settlement; two parties at $15,&0l0, $30,000.
Investigation of lands for general settlement; two parties at $15,000, $30,000.
Retracement of base lines and determination of the position of lines by astronomical observation ; one party at $12,000 and one party at $6,000, $18,000.
Topographical surveys; one party in Manitoba, $8,000; one party in Saskatchewan, $8,000; and two parties in Alberta, $16 000
Miscellaneous surveys by travelling parties-six parties at $6,750, $40,600.

Then there is provision for a re-survey of school lands. That must be continued all the time, and the item is $36,000.
Why is it necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that I can fully explain except to say this:	In
the tremendous amount of surveying that is going on, surveying is called in question all the time, and the school lands surveying, of course, is kept up. Those are trust lands, dealt with separately, and this amount of re-surveying is necessary in connection with school lands. Then there is the survey of the Alberta-British Columbia boundary still going on. Our one-third share of that is $10,000; the provinces pay one-third each, and we pay one-third. The Yukon survey requires $10,000; and then there are timber berths and other surveys unprovided for-we have to survey timber berths now-and the total of that is $20,000.

How are these figures
made up? I would also like a little better explanation from the minister about the lands outside of the fifteen-mile belt. He told us yesterday very definitely that it was not the intention of soldiers to settle on the land that lies more than fifteen miles from a railway. Now he tells us there is $30,000 in this estimate for the examination of lands beyond fifteen miles. I do not know where the lands would be that are only fifteen miles away from a railroad, that are not surveyed. Then as to inspection of the land:	Has not the custom been followed
of having field notes on these lands throughout Western Canada, as was done previously? The field notes of the surveyors have always been very accurate heretofore, and would give the minister a good idea of the nature of the land and the nature of the townships. The townships that are being surveyed must be very far from a railroad -at least the maps of Western Canada show they are surveyed in sections quite a long distance from the railway lines.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The increase is distributed over practically every item. In the first place, each year lately we have had to pay higher wages and to meet a higher cost for supplies. We have diminished the expenditure for surveys to a very low minimum indeed; we had to do it during the war as a necessity and we must now catch up. Consequently the increase is necessary and is spread over all the field work that is required. Soldiers, of course, have a right to go anywhere. They are not confined to the fifteen-mile limit, but that limit is confined for them. They have a right to go

anywhere, and we are doing surveying especially for soldiers in the province of Alberta on a considerable scale. Men are going in in parties and we are having district surveying. Surveying and re-surveying is necessary to take care of their needs. We have always had field notes; that custom has been kept up, but they are not at all sufficient. We have to get better data than that, otherwise tremendous expense will result. The void we propose to fill in the way described.
Has the minister increased the number of parties surveying this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, we have increased the number.
What districts have you covered?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
The minister does not appear to have done very much in the way of making reductions. The whole of the page of the Estimates we are considering appears to be characterized by increases. Out of nineteen items there are large increases in nine and small increases in two. That is not a very satisfactory record in view of the fact that we do not know where we are going to get money to
pay these bills. There is one item in particular I would like the minister to explain, that in regard to parks. 1 have no objection to national parks, I believe in them, but I question whether this is a satisfactory time to increase the expenditure for this purpose by $146,000 in one year. That looks to me like a very extravagant proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has altogether forgotten the drastic reductions that have been made in all these items year after year. Why, it is only a short time since we were spending nearly $700,000 on national parks, but the expenditure has been cut down to about ha'f that amount. Never was the expenditure of any active branch of a public department cut down to such an extent as in that case. Necessarily, now that the war is finished, if we are going to take care of our parks at all, we cannot continue with a minimum expenditure all the time; we have to expend more money more particularly when it costs more to carry out everything we undertake.
Even if we did not give better attention to our parks and employ more men to take care of them, there would be almost that much increase, any way, by reason of the advance in the cost of material and labour. For example, there are roads that we undertook and did not complete; it will never do to leave them incomplete; Oastle-Laggan road-$21,000 for completion of this road; street maintenance-which was allowed to get behind during the war, the Estimates being cut down fifty per cent, necessitating heavy repairs-the increase is $8,000; waterworks and sewer maintenance, $2,000. These also were reduced to the lowest possible minimum. Now the war is over we will have more tourists to Banff park, and we will make more money out of it. For heating plants at stores and administration buildings, we estimate $1,900. This simply means that what was not taken care of in the last two or three years is now being partially or wholly looked after. Improvements in the golf course are estimated to cost $2,000. We charge for the use of the course, and undoubtedly it is a very attractive feature in inducing tourists to use the park.
How much revenue did we receive from the golf course?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been a profit of $200 per year for the past two years.
Good, good!
Are you not afraid of being accused of profiteering?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That was during the blackest period of the war. Will the hon. gentleman now have the item struck out? Stores, $10,000. This is due, in part, to the increase in prices of commodities over prices when last year's estimates were compiled. New cabins, $1,000. This is to improve the fire and game service. Renovations of superintendent's residence, $2,000. Increases in salaries, $3,000. Fire and game protection in Jasper park, $15,000. We will save a lot more than that if we have any measure of increased efficiency at all. Edith Carvell road, $30,000. This is a continuation of work previously started, and will be a valuable asset from a tourist standpoint. The expenditure in Buffalo park-I could go on reading item by item, but I do not think the hon. gentleman really wants that.

I still think the time is inopportune for this expenditure. The minister speaks as if the tide had turned and we were now in a position to embark on expenditure of this kind; but I submit we are not in that position.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is just to take care of work already started.

I submit that there never was a time in the history of the country when it was more im-10 p.m. portant to economize than today. The minister says that in the last few years reductions were made, but now we must embark on these extravagant expenditures. These national parks are pleasure grounds; they are not productive. I have had proposals in my own constituency for productive work; one was a breakwater to give shelter to the fishermen, men who are producing something and helping to pay the national debt. They asked for $10,000 for that purpose. I was told by the minister that I could not get it because "we must economize.'' But I have to go back to my constituency and say, "I sat in a committee that voted $146,000 for building fancy roads through unproductive parks in Western Canada.'' I do not propose to do that without entering my protest. I am not satisfied with the explanation given by the minister, and I submit that these items should not be increased.

I am very sorry to hear the hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair) protest in regard to this expenditure. He classes the national parks of the Dominion as playgrounds. Personally, I am of the opinion that the national parks are just as great assets as	any country can

possibly have, and immense revenues have been derived by every country in the world which has established national parks. The expenditure has been delayed in the Roctky Mountain park-in which Banff is located-during the war, and the expenditure this year is in keeping with the policy of the Government in expenditures on all other works throughout the Dominion. We have a great many returned soldiers located in the Rocky Mountain park and adjacent to it, and one of the objects in expending this money is to furnish employment to those men who may desire to engage in that class of work. These parks induce to come into this country the class of people whom we are very desirous to have come in from every part of the world. In ordeT to visit these parks it is necessary for them to traverse the whole Dominion either from the Atlantic or the Pacific coast, and in the course of these journeys, even though they do go to the parks to spend a short time in pleasure, they get acquainted with the Dominion throughout its whole length, an acquaintance which they could not possibly make iip any other way. There is no doubt that as a result of those trips which are made by people from all parts of the world, many settlers and others are induced to come and spend their hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars in developing the natural resources of this country. I submit that it would be a very shortsighted policy if we were to stop any work projected in the Estimates in connection with our national parks.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would just like to read a compilation made by an official expert on this point. I think it is worth while having it in Hansard:
Publicity experts at the coast place the value of each foreign tourist at $350. This sum covers transportation, hotel and other expenses and is probably a very fair estimate. But allowing for an expenditure by each visitor to the Rockies of only $250, and this includes the ever increasing numbers who remain the entire season and spend many times that much and those who go out with pack trains to the outlying portions of the park who often spend thousands, it is clear that the money brought into Canada by these visitors reaches a very large sum. Take the year 1915, the last year in which owing to war conditions there was a heavy tourist travel from the States. The number of visitors to Rocky Mountain Park in that year was approximately 90,000. Over 65,000 of these visitors were foreigners. Allowing for an expenditure of $250 each it follows that over $16,000,000 of foreign money was brought into Canada by the people of other countries who were attracted to this park, which is just the same as if we had exported goods to those countries and received money in return. Now it is interesting to compare the value on an

acreage basis of our exports of wheat with what we may call our export in scenery. The acreage of Rockir Mountain Park in 1915 was 1,800 square miles or 1,152,000 acres and the value of the foreign tourist traffic it attracted was, roughly speaking, $16,000,000. This works out to a per 'acreage value of $13.88.

Apparently a publicity agent is needed who will give a recommendation for the expenditure of money in certain localities. I agree with my hon .friend from Antigonish and Guysborough that it does seem rather an inopportune time to expend a large 'amount of money on pleasure resorts. We are asked to vote an increase of $146,000 on this item for the maintenance of these national parks at a time when we are facing a very serious financial situation. Like my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair),
I have made application to the Government to expend public money in the Maritime Provinces, but I have met with an absolute refusal because there was no money in the treasury for public buildings or to look after public works, and we were obliged to get along with what we had.
Yet it is proposed to spend this large amount of money on national parks in the western provinces. It is all the harder for hon. members quietly to vote this money when they see that the increase is so very great; we might at least keep the appropriation down to what it was last year. If this vote were thereby reduced by $146,000, we would probably get the same substantial return from the foreigners who visit Canada, but who, no doubt hand over a large amount of money which they spend to the Canadian Pacific railway foi* the carrying of themselves and their families to the points where these parks are located. I hope that the minister will consider seriously the advisability of cutting out some of this large and increased expenditure during the present year.

I notice that in New
Brunswick alone $173,370 is appropriated this year for repairs to wharfs. If we granted to each province all the money they wished for public works, the whole of the national revenue could be allotted to any one province. All we are asking in connection with national parks is Western Canada is that we get a fair share of the money which is to be expended upon public works. The development of the national parks is not dependent only upon expenditures made by the Dominion Government; the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has spent large sums in connection with these parks. The same may be said of the Canadian National railways and of the Grand
Trunk. It is an asset to this country to have these national parks made attractive; the whole of the Dominion receives the benefit.

A very large proportion of
the people of Canada cannot afford to travel over the Canadian Pacific railway for the purpose of visiting these national parks.
I think that the ordinary people should be considered as well as the millionaires.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
knows better than to make an argument of that kind. It is not the people who visit the parks that we are voting this money to; the common people are the people who get the advantage of the money that the tourist spends. We are not voting money to tourists, but if we are to have, parks we must maintain them; we must not let them go to rack and ruin. We have been diminishing our expenditure year after year, while the United States have been increasing theirs, and they have been our competitors in this regard. Their expenditure on this account went up from $150,000 in 1911 to $525,000 last year, in addition to $800,000 by way of railway expenditure; and this year they are jumping from $525,000 to $975,000 for parks, in one department alone, and in another department sufficient to make the total $1,012,205. We have better and more attractive parks to keep up than they have, and we are really getting the business, in spite of all the efforts that they are making. It is not worth while?
Mr. 'COPP: I did not know that it was Canada's ambition to spend money simply because the United States were spending money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Who said it was?

I do not think that the expenditure made by the United States should be the barometer, so to speak, upon the fluctuations of which we base our expenditure in this country. The extra amount that the minister asks for to-night in connection with this work is, in my opinion, altogether out of proportion to the advantage which will result to the people. In respect to the item for the protection of timber in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the railway belt in British Columbia, I assume that the 'Government owns timber areas in these localities. What is the policy of the Government with regard to the method of selling or leasing these timber limits, and what are the returns on that account?

iMr. 'MEIGHEN: The sale is by tender, without exception. The increase, of course, is largely accounted for by the reductions that have taken place in the past; although we have never very much reduced the appropriation for fire protection. While votes connected with practically every other branch were cut down very radically, I did not ask for a reduction last year in the vote for fire protection, because I felt that notwithstanding the fact that we were in the last and worst year of the war, we could not afford to reduce our fire protection organization-that if we did so we might suffer a national loss that would be a hundred times as great as the cost of the protection. There is somewhat of an increase this year because we are now able to get the returned men who were in the service before, competent men who worked with the organization and helped to increase its efficiency. Moreover, we have to pay more for these men now than we formerly paid; we pay $100 a month for new men for fire protection work, and this largely accounts, for the increase. But I have no apologies whatever to make for the size of this vote; if I could proportionately increase the efficiency of the organization by the appropriation of another $100,000 I would cheerfully ask Parliament for the vote. It is very difficult to build up an organization that is anything like an insurance against disastrous fires. Year after year we are managing to work down the percentage of fire losses, although this year we have already had some pretty bad fires. Any vote for this purpose is money well spent so long as we get the very best men, and we spare no efforts to do that.

I agree that our large areas of valuable timber lands should be well protected against loss by fire. May I ask the minister what success the Government has had in connection with tree culture?
Mr. 'MEIGHEN: We have two nurseries out there, one at Indian Head and another at Sutherland, near Saskatoon. We produce thousands of trees for distribution among those who can use them on the farms; on the prairies, broadly speaking, there are no trees at all. More than 50,000,000 of these trees have been distributed and planted with very considerable success. The amount derived from the sale of timber last year was $554,000.

Coming back to parks, does the Government get any direct revenue from these parks other than from a golf course which has already been mentioned?
CMr. Copp.]
Mr. MEIlGHEN: There are many sources of revenue. We do get revenue directly, but of course our revenue directly does not at all equal our expenditure. We could not expect it to do so. The revenue last year from timber licenses and similar sources was $52,000.
iMr. CAMIPBELL: That is just what I want to know, just what items there would be that would give a revenue. The minister has mentioned one; can he mention one or two others?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will give a few items. We, of course, sell some timber in the parks, and the dry timber permits give a revenue. We have some fishing licenses, bath houses, automobile licenses and rentals of lots. For instance, the town of Banff is in the park and the lots upon which the people live are rented from the department.

The last item oh the page is $125,000, to meet uncollected portion of advances of seed grain in the western provinces. Why should we vote money to meet uncollected advances when the money is due to ourselves? Did we not make the advances?
Mr. 'MEIGHEN: I just explained that to the abundant satisfaction of the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb), but I suppose the hon. member (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) was out. We have a new system this year whereby, instead of advancing money to homesteaders directly as has been done for the past forty years, we provide that the banks shall advance the money at 7 per cent interest and take the security; that is, they do not advance any money except on the recommendation and authority of the Dominion land agent of the district who gets the application and finds out the facts. When a bank advances money, we guarantee the bank that it will be repaid with 5 per cent interest if we are called upon to pay it, but if the bank collects the money it collects 7 per cent interest. If we pay, we pay 5 per cent interest to the bank, and we collect 7 per cent interest, and meantime have a lien on our own unpatented land as security for the money. I expect to come out without any loss at all, and also without any administrative expenditure. Hitherto, we have had to keep an organization throughout the country to look after all these seed-grain advances. Now~ we do not need any, the banks doing the work instead, and while we shall not make any money if the man pays-indeed, we pay

the bank 1 per cent for its trouble if it collects the money and saves us all expense 

nevertheless, we shall make money when he does not pay the bank, because ultimately we collect at 7 per cent, whereas, we pay the bank only 5 per cent. I expect the one will balance the other so that we shall come out without any loss.

How much of this $125,000 is represented by grain and how much by expenses?
Mr. MEIGiHEN:	Every five cent piece
is represented by grain. It is just what we may be asked to pay the banks where they call on us and say: We have not been able to collect the money from the farmer; now we want you to pay. This money is lent to the farmer, and when we pay the bank, we take over the security against his crop, but the lien against the land is quite sufficient in itself to protect us against any loss.

Are all the expenses charged?
Mr. MEIGiHEN: There are no expenses. By what I think is a desirable change in policy, we are cutting the expense out and using the banks.

Why does the
item read:
Also including commission payable to banks for collections, fees to secretary-treasurers of municipalities and officers of the provincial Departments of Agriculture, and clerical assistance.
If there are no expenses, what is the meaning of that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think what I have said is- right. I told the hon. gentleman a moment ago that we paid the banks 1 per cent upon what they collected. We are out that, hut against that, we are in the extra money we collect when we collect it over what we pay the bank, namely, the difference between the 5 per cent and 7 per cent upon what we collect. As regards the secretary-treasurers of the municipalities, instead of employing. officers of our own, whom we have formerly had to attend to this work, we use the secretary-treasurer of the municipalities who take applications from the homesteaders and forward them to the Dominion land agent, the secretary-treasurer getting 25 cents for each application he takes and fills out. That is all. It is hardly worth while calling it an expense, but even if it is, it will be offset by the difference between the 5 per cent and the 7 per cent.

I want to revert to the item of surveying. Is it the policy of the Government to continue to survey lands at great distances from railways and to allow settlement upon those lands? The time has come in Canada when we should have some policy governing the settlement of our outlying lands, particularly throughout Western Canada. Settlers are allowed to go in and settle in all parts of that country on any of the lands that are surveyed. In that way we have a little settlement in a district where the land is probably good, which is twenty, thirty, fifty or a hundred miles from a railway, and eventually we shall have to build a railway to that settlement. The Canadian people now own practically the railways of Northern Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, and I have noticed that in the Railway Committee hon. members nave hesitated to grant a charter to the Canadian Pacific or to any other railway company running into the northern part of the Prairie Provinces and the northern part of British Columbia. If we continue to allow settlement on any lands the Dominion Government may own, we are going to have sparse settlement over all our territory; there will be people demanding railways, and we know 'that the Government in power will feel inclined to give a railway to every settlement whether it is a paying proposition or not. We could very well take a section of good territory that could be thrown open for settlement with the understanding that a railway would he built into it, and that no other part of the country would be allowed to be opened for settlement. It is most absurd to allow people to settle even thirty miles from a railway without the possibility of getting a railway, because farming cannot he done successfully at that distance from transportation facilities. Ranchers could go in and make some money, but ranchers take up land on a leasing basis. The Dominion Government should take this matter in hand and not allow settlement scattered over a large	area requiring great mileage of	railways, running through
territory largely owned by speculative land holders, to be built and financed at the expense of the Canadian people. In this connection I should like to bring to the notice of the Government the fact that there are over 10,000 miles of our railway to-day running through non-productive territory, that is, through lands that are held vacant, and this is a very serious burden upon the people of Canada. We have to pay the expenses, and if the Govern-

ment allows promiscuous settlement to continue in Western Canada, the same condition is going to arise again. There will be the expense of building railways, highways, churches and schools and all that goes with settlement, and it would be better to confine settlement to districts where railways exist at present or where they can be built within a reasonable time, so that the settlers may hope to make a success of their venture.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member asks that homesteading be abolished.

I do not want homesteading to be abolished, and the minister knows that. Why then, does he attempt to put words into my mouth? I do not want homesteading to be done promiscuously throughout the country as it has been done in the past. I am not blaming the minister nor this Government for the policy of the past, but the policy has been wrong of allowing people to settle in all parts of the country where the Dominion happens to own land, and I am asking the minister if it is the intention to use some judgment in future as to where he allows people to homestead.
If you are spending $700,000 a year in surveying, you must have some land to survey. The minister told me to-night that it was for homestead purposes. Surely there is some land within this area on which we are spending $700,000 that would be more suitable for homesteading than other parts; for instance, those lands where there are already railroads or where railroads can conveniently be built. I am simply asking that you do not allow settlement to take place in the northern part of Canada when you can put settlers on land where there are railroads or where railroads can be built. I am not advocating the abolition of homesteading by any means.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. gentleman was unnecessarily enraged. I thought he had really advocated the policy of abolishing homesteading. I think he has advocated many other things in the past with far less reason behind them than the abolition of homesteading. I was going to commend his idea, at all events to the extent of saying that there is very good reason behind the advocacy of such a course. There is, of course, a lot to be said the other way. I have canvassed pretty thoroughly and I know the evils the hon. gentleman speaks of, but I am at a loss to know where a man can homestead unless it is on new land. There is not much use
[Mr. Cahill.I
in homesteading if you take away the only land where homesteading can be done, that is, the outlying land, for the rest is all reserved for soldier entry. So, in effect, the hon. gentleman did advocate the abolition of homesteading, in the main at all events; and a lot can be said for that advocacy. I canvassed the situation pretty thoroughly and came to the conclusion that the opinion of those who were nearest to the homestead lands, and who should be the most' interested and the best qualified to judge, was in the main against the abolition of homesteading as yet. It is quite true that the principle of homesteading involves obligations to provide railway facilities for the homesteaders, and that has perhaps resulted in some railway building that might have been delayed. But it is quite false for the hon. gentleman to argue that on account of the homesteading system we have ten thousand miles of railway to-day running through territory that cannot be cultivated. That is owing to a reason very different altogether; it goes back some few years in the history of Canada, with which I do not think the hon. gentleman is altogether unacquainted. But where railways follow homesteaders they go into good territory, not into unsettled territory. It is true that often you have to build railroads ahead of sufficient settlement, and earlier than might have otherwise been necessary, and before the railroad will pay. Homesteading does not bring railways into rocky territory or barren territory; it is only bad politics that does that. So, while perhaps it is too soon to do away with hemesteading, there is a great deal to be said against the policy of permitting homesteading to continue very long in. this country as it has done in the past. At present I have no intention of recommending Parliament to discontinue it; but one of the evils that follows in its wake is not the evil of ten thousand miles of railway through barren territory.

I did not say through barren territory, but through unproductive territory, through territory in a large measure held by speculators in particular. While some of it is more or less barren, the larger part of it is unproductive because it is held by speculators who will not permit settlement.
Would the minister explain this $1,000 vote for the Alpine Club of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Alpine jClub, by their organization, by the spreading of liter-

ture, brings tourists to the country and gets results much more cheaply than we could get them by spending the money direct. The members of the club themselves contribute very largely, the Government very little, and the country gets virtually the whole benefit. I explained this vote before the hon. gentleman came in.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec-Repairs to roads and bridges and drainage, $1,900.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: I wish to draw to the attention of the minister, in order that I may (have a reply from him, a matter that has already been submitted to his department. On the Caughnawaga Indian reserve there is a belt of eight miles leading across the reserve towards the bridge going into Montreal. The roads leading up to the Teserve from the west, the south, and the east are all good macadamized roads, and the contention of the surrounding municipalities is that it is not fair that the Government should not undertake to macadamize this road cross the reserve. As the minister knows, the municipalities have no right to do any work on the reserve. The reserve is under the Government, as the Indians are Government wards, and it is somewhat of a reflection upon the Government's good roads policy that all round the reserve there should be good macadamized roads, built and maintained by the municipalities, while the Government road itself is-I would not like to say a bog, but it is in very poor condition. I should like to know whether the Government proposes to macadamize this eight miles of road this year, so that we shall have' good roads leading into the city of Montreal which will help the farmers get their products into the city.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The matter is in this
shape:	It is no part of the duty of the
Department of Indian Affairs to build roads. If it is the duty of the Dominion Government at all, it pertains to the Department of Public Works. Whether the roads are through an Indian reserve or elsewhere, it is a public work. It is true that municipalities cannot go into the reserve except by consent, but they would have no difficulty in getting consent, as far as that is concerned. The Department of Indian Affairs certainly does not build roads.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
The minister is surely
wrong about that. The Indian Department does build roads. They have an engineer whose special duty it is to look after that work. While I am not authorized to speak officially, I understand from men who are
close to the Quebec Government that they are prepared to contribute something towards the building of this road, but they are powerless to do the work unless the Department of Indian Affairs consents to assist them. The minister knows that the municipality has no right to go in and build roads across an Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We keep an engineer,
it is true, for the purposes of any works that we have to take care of. We take care ot a road through a reserve and see that it is kept in passable shape, but we do not go into anything of this character, or spend $80,000 on macadamizing roads. I do not see that the Government should do so, I do not think that the Department of Public Works has done so, but if any department would do so it would be that department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is merely for keeping the roads through the reserves in order.

speechtext:

Who built the roads the department is taking care of?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am afraid that I am hardly old enough, or historian enough, to tell my hon. friend in this case because this road was built over a hundred years ago. It is the old York road through the Tyendinaga reserve. The other is on the Doncaster reserve. There are no settlers, it appears, on that reserve and the municipality of Ste. Lucie found it necessary to

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say so now.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Does the minister contend that the neighbouring municipalities should go on and do work that really belongs to this Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not belong to us.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Does the minister want it to go out that he thinks this is an obligation of the Department of Public Works, or the Department of Railways and Canals at a time when the Government are boasting that they have a good roads policy? I submit the members should get together and decide who is going to do this work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have never said that anybody should do our work. I merely say as Minister of the Interior that it is not our work and never has been. Work of that character has never been undertaken by the Department of Indian Affairs through any reserve.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: Is it not the minister's duty to see that the department is properly administered? And do not good roads constitute a part of the administration of a reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the building of roads through a reserve is part of the administration of a reserve at all. This is an automobile road to connect up, I understand, with some road from the United States.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: No, with a Canadian road.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, the United States road connects with the Canadian road.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: All roads connect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is a through road. Mr. BUREAU: No.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would not admit the responsibility of the Federal Government, [(Mr. Melghen.]
at least the Department of Indian Affairs, to build that road through an Indian reserve. Roads are not the responsibility of the Federal Government, even though we, as trustees of the Indians or in any other capacity, -might own the land. The roads are not the responsibility of those who own the land, but the roads are a municipal and provincial responsibility.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: If the minister has municipal powers upon the Indian reserve he should see that the Indian Department does its duty.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have proprietary
powers on the .Indian reserve and not municipal powers at all. The hon. gentleman is an owner in his county, but' it is not his duty to build roads. That responsibility is provincial. If it is the duty or responsibility of any governmental authority, it is the province that is responsible. If the province receives assistance from the Dominion it ought to be very grateful, but the responsibility is on the province.

This is all fine argument, but it does not give us the remedy we are claiming. I wish to be serious about this matter. We have an excellent system of highways in the province of Quebec from the boundary line to Montreal, but it so happens that there are two sections of the highway leading into Montreal which constitute permanent obstacles not only to motorists but to those who use the highways for carriages or other vehicles. It is Government property in both cases. The first obstacle is presented by the Indian reserve at Caughnawaga and the second is in the county of Laprairie between the bridge at St. Lambert and St. Constant. The Department of Public Works had formally agreed and promised that that section of the road would be put into proper shape.
The work was started before the election of 1917, and even at an earlier date, after the election of 1911. The road has never been finished and it is a great impediment to persons coming from the city of Montreal on their way to the United States to be stopped at the very gates of that city, because the Department of Public Works does not complete the section of the highway in question. As you come out of that first section you immediately find an excellent highway, but on reaching Caughnawaga, you again find obstacles across that reserve. My hon. friend says this matter should be dealt with by the Department of Public Works. I believe the hon. gentle-

man's statement is true, and that the Department of Public Works ought to build a road across the reserve and complete the other road between the Victoria bridge and the boundaries of Laprairie and St. Constant. It seems to me that although that country does not elect a supporter of the Government regard should be paid to the interests of the travelling public. Seriously speaking, the Minister of the Interior should arrange with the Minister of Public Works to complete that work. I notice that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) has just entered the Chamber. Surely he is familiar with that Laprairie road, and the state it is in, and he should carry out the promise that was made by two or three of his predecessors and, I think, by himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: If my hon. friend will pardon me, I will tell him that the road across the Laprairie dyke is a good deal better than is the road to Montreal. I speak from knowledge, because I was there two weeks ago and noted conditions personally.
Is it finished?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No, it is not finished, and I do not think it ever will be by the way things are going.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I do not know. Perhaps I ought not to say exactly what is in my mind on that matter. In the first place I am very doubtful whether the Dominion Government ever had any license or right to spend a dollar on the work when it was done. When I assumed the duties of office I found that the work going on there was costing about $25 a yard for concrete on force account, and I stopped it. Then I gave another contract. I was not able to get it as early as I should have last year.
Who gave the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:

A contract was given by tender amounting to about $22,000. I was there myself about two or three weeks ago to look over it, and the work was finished, and, as I said before, the service of the road is in better shape to-day than the road from Montreal probably is, or a very great
portion of it. There are certain portions of the dyke which must be finished up and I am going to ask Parliament for sufficient money at this session to finish up the dyke and make it permanent, but as far as I am concerned I propose to ask the province of Quebec to build their own road over the dyke. I do not know that the building of such a road is any of our business, we should never have touched it. Therefore, if my hon. friend wants my views on the matter he is perfectly welcome to have them. Now, as to the Indian reserve, I know nothing whatever about it. I never heard of it before, it is all news to me, and it will take some argument on the part of my hon. friend to convince me that the Public Works Department should go down to the province of Quebec and build any more roads.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Acting Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I desire to give notice to the House that I will move to-morrow for the consent of the House to go on with an Act to amend the Judges' Act which has been on the Order Paper for some time, but which I could not go on with before because a resolution must necessarily precede it. The resolution will be in the Votes and Proceedings to-morrow. I should like to get through to-morrow with the consideration of the resolution if the House will be good enough to consent. I might give the explanation now which is usually given on the introduction of a Bill.
The intention of the Bill is to raise the salaries of the county and district court judges of the Dominion. Those salaries have been for some time $3,000 each, with certain exceptions where they have gone to $3,500 in the case of senior judges. The Bill will raise the salaries of all these county court judges by $1,000, placing them all on the same level of $4,000. It will also raise the salaries of the King's Bench judges of the western provinces and of the Maritime Provinces by $1,000 wherever that is necessary to place them on a level with the salaries of judges of corresponding rank in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The salaries of the judges of Ontario and Quebec will not be affected by this Bill. I thought we should confine the scope of the Bill to such revision as is necessary to take care of those who suffer most from
258i

the increased cost of living 'at the present time. The Bill will also provide for an extra judge for the Exchequer Court of Canada. By virtue of repeated legislative enactments, the work of that court has been increasing rapidly, and if the Divorce Bill now before t(he House passes, will doubtless be very much extended. The Bill increases the salary of the assistant judge of the Exchequer Court by 51,000, placing him in exactly the same position as the puisne judges of the other higher courts of the provinces of the Dominion. The Bill will also provide for denominating the judge of the Exchequer Court the President of the Exchequer Court, as he is denominated, I believe, in England.
There is an additional clause which affects the section that for some years has enabled judges of the higher courts to retire at the expiration of fifteen years on a pension of two-thirds of their salary-a section which has been interpreted as giving to the judge the right to so retire of his own determination. The amendment has the effect of providing that that option may only he exercised when in the opinion of the Governor in Council it can be exercised in the public interest. That revision, however, will have no retroactive effect; i't will only affect future appointments.

My hon. friend said that the judges in the Western and the Maritime Provinces will be on the same footing in regard to salary as the judges of Ontario and Quebec.
Mr. T^EIG'HEN: My hon. friend will pardon me. I should not have said the Maritime Provinces, but the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The Bill does, however, raise the salary of the Chief Justice of Prince Edward Island up to $6,500 and the Puisne judges to $5,500, and does away with all additional salaries to admiralty judges on the expiration of the ten years of office of the present holders of those positions. It also does away with the salaries of the judges of the courts of divorce from the present day.

My hon. friend said that these judges wrould be put on a footing of equality as regards salary with the judges of Ontario and Quebec. Will it be on a footing of equality with Quebec or Ontario, because there is a difference? A judge of the Superior Court in Ontario receives $1,000 more than a judge of the Superior Court in Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know they are not precisely parallel, bu't taken on the whole the [<Mr. Meighen.]
salaries of the judges of Ontario and Quebec are the same. You cannot parallel one bench exactly against the other, but taking it all in all, I think they are as closely equal as could be made. That at all events is the intention and those were the instructions given to Mr. Newcombe, who prepared the Bill. Apparently he arrived at the same conclusion.

speechtext:
Before referring to section ' 325 it will be necessary for the hon. gentleman to have the unanimous consent of the Committee. Is it the unanimous will of the Committee that the hon. member be allowed to revert to section 325 of the Bill?
Mr. McQuarrie: I can go on with it now or wait until the third reading. It will take me a few minutes to explain it, but if the Committee do not wish me to go on to-night I shall defer what I have to say until the third reading. The amendment to section 325 has the effect 01" practically wiping out all agreements made between municipalities and the railway companies fixing rates in those municipalities.
It also has the effect of wiping out an appeal which is now pending to the Supreme Court.
I want to explain these things to the Committee, but if you would prefer me to do it on the third reading I should be glad to postpone what I have to say. It is so late now that I do not like to keep the Committee, but if you wish me to go ahead I am prepared to do so.
This was at one o'clock in the morning.
Mr. J. D. Reid: I have no objection, but I do not like to ask the Committee to remain.
Mr. McQuarrie: That is the way I feel, too. Mr. J. D. Reid: Does the hon. member wish to have the clause opened up again?
Mr. McQuarrie: Yes.
Mr. J. D. Reid: I would not like to have the clause opened up again. Rather than have the clause opened I would prefer that you bring it up on the third reading.
Mr. McQuarrie: I will take it up on the third reading, then.
After leaving the House that same night I saw the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) and asked him if the Bill .were coming up next day. He said " No." I said: " Can I rely on that?" And he said " Yes." I said " Very well; I have a lot of other things to do, very important matters to attend to, and I will probably not be in the House to-morrow." He said " All right." I said further " Will you inform me when this Bill is coming before the House so that I can take it up?" And he said " Yes." The Minister of Railways knew how important it was to certain of my constituents that it should not go through in the form in which it was at that time. Next day the Budget debate went off suddenly, unexpectedly, no doubt, and I * learned that the Minister of Railways had brought on the third reading of the Bill when there was practically no one in the House except a bare quorum, and that the Bill had been passed.
I am a supporter of this Government but at the same time I do not think that I am entitled as a member of this House to be treated in that manner. I was told that when this matter came back from the Sen-

ate I would then have an opportunity ol making my motion to refer the Bill back to the committee, that the motion would be in order and that that would be the proper time for me to make it. Now I am ruled out of order. I, of course, have to accept the ruling of the Speaker. I would like to say something on this amendment to section 325.
This amendment was first inserted in the Bill when it was before the special committee which, as hon. gentlemen know, was appointed to consider the Consolidated Railway Act this session. It did not appear in the Bill as submitted by the Senate to us but was inserted when the measure was before the special committee. Now I have been wondering why there was this unseemly haste in rushing this amendment through; why the thing was kept more or less secret, and no publicity given to it. Nobody-very few members of the House in any event - knew anything about this amendment, or comprehended the effect of it. The only explanation of the unseemly haste that occurs to me is that the minister knew and realized that if anybody became aware of the purport and effect of the amendment there would be a great deal ot opposition to it. This is now subsection 5 of section 325:
Notwithstanding the provisions of section 3 the powers given to the Board under this Act to fix, determine, land enforce just and reasonable rates and to change and' alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require, shall not be limited, or in any m'annr affected by the provisions of any Act of the Parliament of Canada, whether general in application or special and relating only to any specific railway or railways, and the board shall not excuse any charge of unjust discrimination whether practised against shippers, consignees, or localities, or of undue or unreasonable preference, on the ground that such discrimination or preference is justified or required by any agreement made or entered into by the company.
Now section 325 deals with the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and without this proposed amendment there is a doubt as to whether the board would have jurisdiction to determine or allow rates which exceed the rates fixed in agreement made with railway companies by municipalities and other corporations, or which may have been fixed by statute or agreements ratified by statute. The effect of this, amendment, as I have said, is practically to wipe out all those agreements, and in the case of a certain municipality it has the effect of wiping out an appeal which is now pending to the Supreme Court of Canada. That appeal was brought by the municipality of 
Burnaby, a municipality situated between the cities of Vancouver and New Westminster. That municipality had an agreement with the electric railway company which operates three lines through it that in consideration of certain privileges which were granted by the municipality to the railway * company, the latter should not, on certain of its lines in that municipality, charge more than certain specified fares. One of these lines is known as the Burnaby Lake or Fraser Valley line. That line comes within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and as to it there was the agreement to which I have referred. The company after receiving and obtaining the privileges to which it was entitled under that agreement, made application to the Board of Railway Commissioners to approve an increased tariff of fares, which fares in some cases exceeded by one hundred per cent those mentioned in the agreement. When the matter came before the Board of Railway Commissioners, in August of last year, the municipality opposed the application, but after reserving judgment the board handed down a decision holding that they had the right and the jurisdiction to allow the increased tariff, notwithstanding the agreement in question. The point was raised at the hearing that the board had no jurisdiction to entertain that application, and as to that question, which was one of law, the board agreed to allow an appeal to be taken to the Supreme Court of Canada. I have here a letter from the board dated November 26, 1918, which reads as follows:
File 2>S 4>3'9, Appl'n of B.C. Electric Ry.
Co., re increase in Commutation fares.
Dear Sirs,-Referring to your telegram of the 2i3rd inst., I wired you yesterday, by night lettergram, under the Board's direction as follows :
" Tour wire twenty-third instant. Board will facilitate appeal to Supreme Court on defined question or questions of law. This permission will not operate as a stay." Tours truly,
,	Secretary, B.R.C.
Now in order that there may be no doubt as to the reasonableness of the appeal of the municipality, or as to the occasion for it, I will read a short extract from the ruling of the chief commissioner, given on the 30th of J anuary last:
In view of the fact that the municipality desires to raise the question of the board's power to deal with any question as against the terms of its agreement, and the further fact that the practice of the board is to grant leave to appeal on any legal point that is open to reasonable controversy, it is necessary that the

question of the applicability of the agreement should be determined.
That appeal has not yet come before the Supreme Court of Canada, because the question of law has not yet been finally settled by the Board of Railway Commissioners; if this amendment is passed, the municipality will not have the right to take its case to the Supreme Court, and this appeal will necessarily fail.
The wording of the amendment may not make that perfectly clear, but I have it on the authority of no less a person than Sir Henry Drayton himself. He tells me that he has reserved handing down his decision in this matter as to the question of law to be submitted until Parliament shall have finally disposed of this Bill and this particular amendment.
Now, my reason for speaking to-night is that I feel I cannot agree to the motion before the House, namely, that this section 325 should be passed as it now stands. I wish to have the privilege of moving an amendment to protect the rights of municipalities in the case of agreements which give railway companies' certain privileges and on the other hand provide
12 m. that the railway companies' fares shall not exceed certain specified amounts. I think that those municipal rights should be protected, or, if they are not protected, and if the railway companies are allowed to escape from their covenants under those agreements some provision should be made to cancel the privileges which they obtained from the municipalities. I understand from both the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works that when this Bill comes before the House again it will be quite in order for me to move this amendment, and I intend to accept that privilege.
